inline.s: There is a further point. If beings understood that emptiness and existence are simultaneous, they would see that emptiness and existence alike are beyond all speaking; and if they understood that emptiness and existence are not yet fit to be spoken of, what use would they have for discrimination? This is the subtle intent with which the Buddha spoke of emptiness and existence as simultaneous. For it serves both to remove the discriminating views and feelings of beings and to lead them to leave behind names and words and realize for themselves. Hence whether one speaks of existence or of non-existence, of both existence and non-existence, or of neither existence nor non-existence, all alike is relinquished. The above is spoken from the standpoint of the remedy. If one speaks thoroughly from the standpoint of the ultimate meaning, then when relinquishing is spoken of, all is relinquished; when non-relinquishing is spoken of, nothing is relinquished. One should know that whenever relinquishing is spoken of, it is because of grasping that there is relinquishing. If there is nothing grasped, there is nothing to relinquish. Therefore even the simultaneity of emptiness and existence must not be grasped, and grasping itself should be relinquished. How do we know this is so? Consider the Heart Sutra: it first says that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, making clear the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, so that people may awaken to it and enter the right wisdom of prajna. Yet further on it says, "no wisdom and no attainment." This is precisely the instruction that even the simultaneity of emptiness and existence should not be grasped. This sutra says so plainly as well, as when it says that prajna is not prajna. The same holds in this very section: above it says that the true mark is then produced and merit accomplished, yet this section says the true mark is precisely non-mark and is named the true mark. It is again to guard against people grasping at the true mark that it speaks of "not" and says "is named," thereby relinquishing it. The true mark is precisely the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. One should know why the simultaneity of emptiness and existence must not be grasped. Because if there is the least grasping, one leans to the side of existence and it is no longer the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. Hence it should be relinquished. And if one hears these words of mine yet does not in the least comprehend and contemplate the meaning of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, then one leans to the side of emptiness, and it is again no longer the simultaneity of emptiness and existence; this too should be relinquished. One should comprehend it in this way. This is of the utmost importance.

In short, if the views and feelings of beings are emptied, one may speak of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, and may as well speak of the four propositions; but if they are not emptied, then the four propositions certainly may not be spoken, and the simultaneity of emptiness and existence likewise cannot be granted. Pay attention, pay attention!

In the second meaning of the true mark spoken of above it is said that this section and the preceding text, "if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata," illuminate each other. From this the elder's deep understanding of the meaning may also be seen. Yet what the elder deeply understood does not stop here. One should know that the nature has many other names. Not citing others, he cites the one name "true mark" alone; this too illuminates the meaning of the teachings above that dharmas and non-dharmas alike should not be grasped, that non-dharmas are not non-dharmas, that what is spoken is not the name, and so on. All that the World-Honored One spoke above was to keep people from grasping at either of the two extremes of emptiness and existence and thus to make all perfectly fused. For to grasp at the two extremes is to be no longer nature but mark. If one grasps at the mark of dharma, that is grasping at self; if one grasps at the mark of non-dharma, that too is grasping at self. Now the elder, even with respect to the true mark in which emptiness and existence are simultaneous, likewise says it is not and is named. This is precisely aimed at what the World-Honored One spoke above, illuminating two meanings for him so that the hearer may comprehend. What are the two meanings? (1) The nature is from the first the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence (the word "simultaneous" means perfectly fused). If one grasps at the two extremes, one is no longer in accord with the nature. (2) Even the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence should not be grasped, for if there is the least grasping it is no longer the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, to say nothing of the two extremes, which still less should be grasped. This is the deep intent of citing the true mark alone, and this is precisely why the elder deeply understood the meaning.

Again, as was said above, the word "not" in this section carries the sense of "free from," and it speaks of the work of cultivation. It corresponds to the section below, that one who is free from all marks is then named a Buddha. One should know that these two sections, the one encouraging by way of the present and the one encouraging by way of the future, are nowhere out of correspondence. For what the two sections say was from the first meant to illuminate each other. This meaning will be spoken of below.

(Zi) Next, encouraging by way of the future. It divides into two: (Chou) 1. Rejoicing now and encouraging those who come after; 2. Explaining and revealing the reason. (Chou) 1. Again divides into two: (Yin) 1. Rejoicing for himself; 2. Extensive encouragement.
(Yin) 1. Rejoicing for himself.
["World-Honored One, that I now hear such a sutra, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it — this is not difficult."]

"That I now hear such a sutra, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it" — this single phrase explains precisely why it is that the wisdom-eye he had gained in former times had never before heard such a sutra. Why? If one knows that he now hears it and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, one knows that his not having heard it before was due to nothing else: there was a wisdom-eye he had gained, and that very wisdom-eye produced its own obstruction to this profound sutra. Even had he heard it, he could not have believed, understood, received, and upheld it; he would have heard as though he had not heard. Hence he says that the wisdom-eye he had gained had never heard it. These words explain precisely that the whole obstruction lay in the wisdom-eye. How could the wisdom-eye produce obstruction? It was entirely because there was something gained. Why so? To have something gained is the grasping at dharmas; it is shallow and short wisdom. How then could one accord with this supreme meaning of the three emptinesses? Moreover, to have something gained is to feel that one's own enlightenment already suffices; it is to have no breadth of compassionate vows. How then could one accord with this wondrous practice of giving oneself up for others, ferrying others yet with no mark of ferrying? This is why in former times he had never heard it. Now, however, he had glimpsed the World-Honored One's total non-dwelling and his eye of the Way opened; for the sake of the assembly he asked that this profound sutra be spoken, and his great mind was aroused. Hence he could hear it and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it.

To understand is to comprehend. To receive is to take in, which is also to comprehend. Thus understanding and receiving are close in meaning. Since it says understanding and then says receiving, the two words "receive and uphold" are spoken together; for speaking them together makes clear that one should advance in understanding and practice side by side. Again, the word "uphold" also carries the sense of holding without loss. So the phrase "believe, understand, receive, and uphold" makes clear that one can not only believe and understand but can advance in understanding and practice together without retreating. "Not difficult" means not very difficult; it does not mean absolutely not difficult. That it is not very difficult is precisely why he rejoices for himself. Had it been absolutely not difficult, he could not have said that in former times the wisdom-eye had never heard it, nor would he have shed tears and wept and praised it as rare.

Why is it not difficult? There are three meanings. (1) His person met the time of a Buddha. With instruction given to his face and whispers in his ear, benefit came easily. Moreover, by the Tathagata's clear receiving, merely to see and hear and rejoice brings the greatest of blessings and gives rise to the greatest of wisdom, without any instruction being needed. And to be born into such a great assembly, one's former roots of blessing and wisdom must surely be deep. With causes and conditions thus complete, whenever the Buddha spoke the Dharma, those who realized the fruit on the spot could not be numbered. But to be born before the Buddha or after him is one of the eight difficulties. The elder was himself one of the great disciples, so he says it is not difficult. This is the first reason he rejoices for himself. (2) He had already realized the fruit of sagehood. The Great Prajnaparamita says: "Prajna is most profound; who can believe it? Answer: one who has accomplished right view, and the arhat whose outflows are exhausted, can believe it." Now the elder had already realized the fruit of arhatship, so it is not difficult. This is the second reason he rejoices for himself. (3) He could understand the meaning of emptiness. The whole prajna corpus makes clear the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and among the ten great disciples the elder was foremost in understanding emptiness. His nature was the sharpest and he entered most easily. Hence in the first eight assemblies the elder was the one who received the teaching, and now it is again the elder who sets this most profound sutra in motion. So he says it is not difficult. This is the third reason he rejoices for himself.

Looking over the text below, all these meanings are present as well. Why? The elder's own words that it is not difficult serve precisely to reveal how utterly difficult it is for the final age, since those beings are born when no Buddha is met. And where he rejoices for himself is precisely where he redoubles his encouragement of those who come after. The sense is: I am fortunate enough now to meet the World-Honored One, I have realized arhatship and understand the meaning of emptiness, and so I can believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. But those beings of the final age, meeting no Buddha and finding it very hard to hear and very hard to believe, understand, receive, and uphold — if they nonetheless hear, and can nonetheless believe, understand, receive, and uphold, they are truly rare and precious, and their capacities must far surpass my own (for bodhisattva-nature far surpasses arhat-nature). What is there remarkable in me? Hence he says it is not difficult. In these few lines the wording and sense turn and return with earnest urgency; how wholeheartedly he strives to inspire those who come after!
(Yin) 2. Extensive encouragement.
["If in a future age, in the last five hundred years, there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such persons will be foremost and most rare."]

"A future age" speaks broadly of the time after the Buddha. "The last five hundred years" refers to the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Buddha's entry into stillness, that is, the very beginning of the Dharma-ending age. Now it is nearly three thousand years, already at the end of the sixth five-hundred-year period. Wherever the sutras speak of "the last five hundred years," it is not necessarily the fifth; the phrase simply makes clear that it is the Dharma-ending age. The Surangama Sutra says that at this time beings are firm and solid in contention, and entry upon the Way is very difficult. "Contention" means affirming oneself and denying others, striving for superiority and fighting to win. "Firm and solid" means that contention is unrelenting and unbreakable. Consider how in China since the Song dynasty (from the early Song to the present is nearly a thousand years; that time was precisely the beginning of the Dharma-ending age) those devoted to moral cultivation and learning carried on sectarian quarrels far exceeding those of the Han and Tang. Thus arose the tendency of Song learning to reject Han learning, and the habit of Confucians to slander Buddhism. Later the so-called Neo-Confucians began contending among themselves, as with the two factions of the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools. In every case it was nothing but planting one's own banner and striking down others. Cause must have its effect: in the end they were themselves struck down by others, and so came the movement that overthrew old learning together with the new, in which even Confucius was dragged down. They did not realize that since the Han dynasty no scholar has even dreamt of Confucius's true meaning. And within the Buddhist gate itself, after the Song the same tendency took hold; the various schools and factions contended fiercely, each holding its own school alone to be right and all others wholly wrong. The further it went, the worse it became, until in recent times some have wished to overthrow the Awakening of Faith. This is truly lamentable. If even the Buddhist gate is like this, and those devoted to morals and learning are like this, what of the rest? Hence the word "struggle" has become a motto. They do not realize that the ancients spoke of "striving," of "exerting oneself," of "self-strengthening"; even in Buddhism one speaks of "courage" and "vigor." Such expressions all refer to one's own person and are beneficial without fault. Today's "struggle," though also a kind of self-strengthening, carries the intent of excluding others. This comes from the habitual tendency to contention growing ever deeper, and it is why the world's way grows ever more bitter.

Whence does contention arise? It arises from grasping. Grasping comes from discrimination, and discrimination from the view of self, and the Buddha Dharma is the specific remedy for this disease. Now the World-Honored One and the elder both encourage people specifically with regard to the Dharma-ending age. From this it can be known that to remedy people's minds today and turn back the world's fortune, there is no way but to promote the Buddha Dharma, for it is precisely the fitting remedy for the illness. Yet precisely because it fits the illness, it runs counter to human sentiment. For those who are firm in contention have deep obstacles and heavy karma; their inner causes are clearly incomplete. Add that the sages are distant in time and good teachers are few, so the outer conditions are likewise insufficient. With both cause and condition lacking, in the case of this profound sutra, not only is receiving and upholding difficult, not only is believing and understanding difficult; even to hear it is already very difficult. It is not that there is no opportunity at all to hear the Dharma; it is that people are unwilling to hear. If then there are those free of these three difficulties, they must have long planted good roots, or must have been sent by the Buddha. Therefore it says, "they will be foremost and most rare," making clear that such a person is either a bodhisattva's manifestation or one who possesses bodhisattva-nature.

"Will be" means "shall be," and carries within it the sense of accomplishment. Someone may object: a bodhisattva's manifestation aside, how could one who merely possesses bodhisattva-nature accomplish this? One should know that the sutra first says "hears," then says "believes, understands, receives, and upholds," making clear that the three wisdoms are complete in him. How could he not accomplish it? Hearing is the wisdom of hearing; believing and understanding is the wisdom of reflection; receiving and upholding is the wisdom of cultivation. For to dwell in the final age and yet hear this profound sutra is truly no easy matter; such a one must have prajna seeds from former lives, one of whom it is said, "not merely before one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas did he plant good roots." Only with such a surpassingly good cause can one meet so surpassingly good a condition. So hearing it, he can at once give rise to faith and open understanding. There are, now and then, those who though they hear it meet some other obstructing condition, so that their faith cannot at once be fully aroused and their understanding cannot open widely; but if only they follow the Buddha's command, keep the precepts and cultivate merit, they will surely come to believe, understand, receive, and uphold. For keeping the precepts cuts off defiling conditions; this is the foundation of self-benefit. Cultivating merit unfolds the virtues of the nature (since the nature inherently possesses immeasurable pure virtues); this too is the work of benefiting others. Thus turning the back on dust and uniting with enlightenment (cutting off defiling conditions is "turning the back on dust"; unfolding the virtues of the nature is "uniting with enlightenment"), benefiting both self and others, one will surely receive the welcoming of all Buddhas, and from this one can give rise to faith in this sutra and take it as real. "Take it as real" means to understand its true meaning. Believing and understanding, one will naturally receive and uphold it in accord with the Dharma. With the three wisdoms thus cultivated together, what fear is there that one will not accomplish it? Again, in the words "such a person will be foremost and most rare" there lies the sense that one must not cast oneself away. This is the elder's earnest encouragement. This sentence echoes the words above, "you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue," and the words below, "then he is named a Buddha," exactly corresponding to them.

(Chou) 2. Explaining and revealing the reason. In three parts: (Yin) 1. Directly revealing that he does not grasp at existence; 2. Bending back to reveal that he does not grasp at emptiness; 3. Concluding by revealing that he is named a Buddha.
(Yin) 1. Directly revealing that he does not grasp at existence.
["Why? Such a person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life."]

The text above says such a person is foremost and most rare. How does he come to be so? The three sections that follow explain precisely why. In the circulating editions the word "no" is added before each mark, but the Tang manuscript sutras run "no mark of self" straight through, so the three "no"s below may be omitted.

"Why?" puts a hypothetical question: why is such a person called foremost and most rare? The answer: because in such a person the four marks of self, person, being, and life are all absent. Being all absent, he does not grasp at existence. Judging by the surface of the text, it seems only to say that he is empty of the marks of self and person, and seems only to make clear that he does not grasp at existence. But looking at the bending-back revelation below, such a person is not only empty of self and person, but also empty of dharma-self; not only does he not grasp at existence, he does not grasp at emptiness either. Yet the section heading says only "does not grasp at existence" because it follows the surface of the text; the meaning of not grasping at emptiness cannot be known without the bending-back revelation of the next section.

One should know that this sutra is devoted to making clear the true mark. The true mark is absolute, with nothing outside it, and is from the first no mark at all. What is called the relinquishing of both self and dharma, and non-grasping at emptiness and existence, is this. "The relinquishing of both self and dharma" means that the four marks of self, person, and the rest are all thoroughly relinquished. "Non-grasping at emptiness and existence" means that marks such as those of self and dharma are not grasped, which is not grasping at existence, and is also called the emptiness of self and the emptiness of dharmas; and that non-dharma marks are also not grasped, which is not grasping at emptiness, and is also called the emptiness of emptiness. Together with the two emptinesses of self and dharma, these are called the three emptinesses. Beings of the final age must possess prajna-nature and have relatively thin grasping at self and dharma before they can, in this turbid and evil world, hear this Dharma; only then can they rise above the common run and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. And being able to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, their grasping at the emptiness and existence of self and dharma is relinquished of itself. This is why such a person is precisely a foremost and most rare bodhisattva. Hence the words "will be" above contain the sense of accomplishment. For this reason.
(Yin) 2. Bending back to reveal that he does not grasp at emptiness.
["Why is this? The mark of self is precisely non-mark; the mark of person, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are precisely non-mark."]

"Why is this?" asks of himself the reason for the word "no" in the text above. From "the mark of self" onward he answers and explains himself. The sense is that the "no" just spoken is not "no" as opposed to "yes"; it is absolute nothingness, the nothingness of all four propositions, that is, emptiness carried through to the very bottom. How is this shown? Because such a person has not seen self, person, being, and life as truly existent and then been able to be without them, still less has he annihilated self, person, being, and life and then been without them. He is able to see that the self is from conditions, illusorily existing, and that when its illusory mark appears it is precisely non-existent; hence he says the mark of self is precisely non-mark. This sentence makes clear that he does not take up emptiness apart from the mark of self. The mark of person, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life being precisely non-mark is likewise so. The Great Treatise says: "If there were a single hair-tip of what beings grasp that could exist, it could not be left behind; but since in what is grasped there is not so much as a hair's breadth of existence, it can be left behind." The sense is that all is illusory mark, and there is from the first not a hair-tip's worth that truly exists. It makes clear precisely that existence itself is emptiness, and that is why it can be left behind. It is like one with a film over the eye seeing flowers in space: where the flowers are is where space is. Why bother to destroy the flowers and take up space apart from them? When the film is cleared the flowers vanish of themselves, and this is likewise so.

Spoken of the nature: if one understands the one true dharma-realm, then there is from the first no difference, from the first constant and everlasting; how could there be marks of self, person, being, and life? Spoken of marks: if one understands that the five aggregates are from the first empty, then one knows that when the mark of self appears, that is precisely when it is empty; hence the mark of self is precisely non-mark. And the mark of person and all marks of beings are likewise nothing but the false union of the five aggregates, from the first empty; hence the mark of person and the mark of a being are likewise precisely non-mark. As for what is called the mark of a life, it is because its continuity is unbroken that this mark is formed. But in truth, since it is called continuity, one can see that it is thought after thought flowing on, arising and ceasing in a single instant; is not the mark of a life precisely non-mark? Such a person, believing, understanding, receiving, and upholding, is able to be thus, and so possesses the wisdom of the three emptinesses and is free of the four propositions as well. Why? If one cannot thoroughly penetrate that self, person, being, and life are from the first illusory marks, appearing though not existent, then even if one can be non-grasping, it is forced suppression, that is, a "no" set against "yes." The insight being still untrue, not only is the effort laborious, but the root and stem remain and it is utterly unreliable. And even if one could suppress without slackening, that too is grasping at dharmas. As the Surangama Sutra says: even if one inwardly guards the secluded and still, that too is a shadowy affair of the discriminating dust of dharmas. The fault lies in the one word "guard": where there is something guarded, there is something grasped. Why is this so? Because the insight is not thorough. Now this person has thoroughly seen that marks such as those of self and others are precisely non-mark; he can penetrate clearly that all marks, being existent, are precisely non-existent. Existing yet non-existent, he sees as though not seeing. Though the myriad forms are myriad and tangled, his breast is serene. Then without suppression they vanish of themselves; what use is guarding? Where there is nothing guarded, there is nothing grasped; this is freedom from the mark of dharma. Moreover it is not merely the emptiness of dharmas: the mark of self being precisely non-mark, one can see that he does not take up emptiness apart from marks; this is also freedom from the mark of non-dharma. Is this not emptiness of emptiness as well? The emptiness of self, the emptiness of dharmas, and the emptiness of emptiness: this is wisdom penetrating the three emptinesses. Hence the title of this section says "not grasping at emptiness." Such a person is truly of great capacity, for he can empty through to the very bottom and is not one who works away at it twig by twig and joint by joint.

It was said above that he is free of the four propositions as well; what does that mean? The section above has him not grasping at existence and this section has him not grasping at emptiness, which makes clear that he is free of both existence and non-existence. And it says that the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark. Since it says "precisely," one can see that such a person does not regard existence and non-existence as both existing and not existing, or as neither existing nor not existing, kept apart and unfused. Rather, he has seen that existence is precisely non-existence. Then his wisdom is already thorough, and emptiness and existence are simultaneous; is he not free of the four propositions? The self-nature pure mind is from the first free of the four propositions, neither mark nor non-mark, absolute and perfectly fused. This person now transcends the four propositions, is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty, perfectly fused without obstruction, and so has entered into the nature-substance of the true mark. Hence it says he will be a foremost and most rare bodhisattva. The next section precisely concludes and reveals this meaning.
(Yin) 3. Concluding by revealing that he is named a Buddha.
["Why? One who is free from all marks is then named a Buddha."]

"Why?" asks: since the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark, why is he called foremost and most rare? The two lines "free from all marks" explain the reason. "All marks" are precisely self, person, being, and life. Marks are not one only, hence "all." And it further says "all" because it is not merely that the four marks of self and the rest arise from the view of the body. The text above says: if one grasps at the mark of dharma, or grasps at the mark of non-dharma, one grasps at self, person, being, and life. It can be seen that whatever is grasped becomes the four marks; hence "all." Spoken in terms of the four propositions: one may grasp at existence, or grasp at non-existence, or grasp at both existence and non-existence, or grasp at neither existence nor non-existence. Where there is grasping, there is grasper and grasped; grasper and grasped are opposition, and opposition becomes the marks of self and other. Since the graspings are not one, they become the mark of a being; since the grasping mind does not cease, it becomes the mark of a life. Hence "all marks." The nature of the true mark is from the first free of both marks and non-marks. So if one can be free of all marks, one realizes the dharma-body; hence, "is then named a Buddha."

"All Buddhas" has two meanings. (1) The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. (2) From the first abiding onward, up to but not including the ultimate fruition, they are called those who awaken in part, and also called Buddhas of partial realization, because they can realize the dharma-body in part. From the first abiding to the ultimate enlightenment is forty-two stages in all; hence "all Buddhas." Spoken in the first sense, it means that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times all obtain the name Buddha by being free from all marks. This person has already cut off the four propositions and penetrated the three emptinesses; he is free from all marks. Though he has not at once reached the ultimate Buddha-stage, he is unquestionably a bodhisattva. Hence it says only "foremost and most rare," not "the supreme, foremost, and most rare." Spoken in the second sense, from the first-abiding bodhisattva of partial realization upward to the ultimate enlightenment, all must be free from all marks in order to realize the dharma-body. This person can be free from all marks; he has already realized the dharma-body. Though we do not know how deep or shallow his realization is, at the least he is a first-abiding bodhisattva and a Buddha of partial realization. He is also one whose faith is pure, so that the true mark is produced and he accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue. Hence it says he will be foremost and most rare.

What is said here, that the mark of self is precisely non-mark and so forth, is the non-duality of emptiness and existence, the perfect fusion of nature and mark. It is also the confluence of all the meanings spoken by the World-Honored One above. Why? Because to be free from all marks is then to be named a Buddha, which corresponds from afar to what the section on generating faith says: if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata. So it is enough to prove that this person, able to be free from all marks, has already seen the Tathagata's nature-substance; is he not foremost and most rare? The insight the elder sets forth is truly mind-to-mind with the World-Honored One; this is what is meant by deeply understanding the meaning. Hence below the World-Honored One at once confirms it.

It was said above that these three sections encouraging by way of the future and the two sections above encouraging by way of the present illuminate each other in meaning. Consider how the earlier text speaks only of the one word "faith," while here it says "believe, understand, receive, and uphold." This is precisely to illuminate that the earlier text, though it spoke only of faith, already included the sense of understanding and receiving and upholding; for faith is the mother of the merit and virtue that are the source of the path. To speak the one word "faith" is to run through to the very end. That here it speaks of being without all marks again illuminates the reason why the earlier text says that when faith is pure the true mark is produced. And that mark is precisely non-mark, non-grasping at the two extremes, the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, is precisely the true exposition of the true mark. That here it says he will be foremost and most rare, and is named a Buddha, is likewise the meaning of the earlier text's accomplishing the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue. Here it says "free from," and above it said "not": the two precisely answer each other, for since marks and non-marks alike are not, one should be free of them. Above it says "produces the true mark," and again says "the Tathagata says it is named the true mark"; here it says "is then named a Buddha." The meaning too is one thread. For to manifest a portion of the Tathagata's true mark is to be a Buddha of partial realization; to manifest it in full is the ultimate Buddha. And that both before and after it says "named" again makes clear that what is called the true mark, and what is called all Buddhas, are both mere names and therefore neither may be grasped. Hence all must be "not" and all must be "free from." From this one sees that before and after there is only one meaning. So when speaking the earlier text one should include the later meaning, and when speaking the later text one should include the earlier meaning. One is spoken by way of the present and the other by way of the future, each making the other manifest; this again is the skill of Dharma-speaking. Such a pattern is met with constantly in the sutras.
(Ren) Next, the Tathagata's confirmation and unfolding. In three parts: (Gui) 1. Confirming; 2. Unfolding the meaning; 3. Concluding.
(Gui) 1. Confirming.
[The Buddha told Subhuti: "So it is, so it is. If again there are persons who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such persons are most rare."]
To confirm is to approve what the elder said; to unfold is, on the basis of what the elder said, further to make clear the meanings above that were not yet exhausted.

Wherever the line "the Buddha told Subhuti" is set down, it carries a note of solemnity. Because the text below mostly supplies what the earlier meaning had not yet brought out, the compiler of the sutra specially marks this line to draw attention to it. That "so it is, so it is" is said twice confirms that his words are entirely apt. If one distributes the sense, it means that the praise and rejoicing above and the extensive encouragement are both without error. The elder earlier said, "If again there are persons," without yet indicating any particular time; but because it stood opposite the next section's encouragement by way of the future, it was judged to be encouragement by way of the present. Now the World-Honored One likewise says only "if again there are persons," also without being able to specify a time; yet when the text below comes to its conclusion it returns to the future. From this it can be known that these words refer generally to the present and on to the future.

To be startled is to be suddenly amazed and bewildered; to be terrified is to be anxious and unsettled; to be afraid is to draw back and obstruct oneself. Vasubandhu's Treatise says: "Startled means fearing that this sutra is not the practice of the right path; terrified means being unable to cut off doubt; afraid means that because of being startled and terrified one is unwilling to study and practice it." Zhiyi's Commentary says: "At first hearing the sutra one is not startled; next, reflecting on its meaning, one is not terrified; afterward, practicing it, one is not afraid." Taking treatise and commentary together, not being startled is faith; for when first hearing the sutra, not fearing that it is not the right path and so being startled is to be able to believe. Not being terrified is understanding; for next reflecting on the meaning, to have no doubt at all and so give rise to terror is to be able to understand. Not being afraid is receiving and upholding; for not drawing back in fear and so being willing to study and practice is to be able to receive and uphold. That the wording is changed here holds a deep meaning. Truly, when ordinary beings who grasp at existence hear that all marks are false and delusory, and when the two vehicles, grasping at dharmas, hear that dharmas should not be grasped, and when those of a certain lean-to-emptiness sort hear that non-dharmas likewise should not be grasped, they are sure to be startled and terrified and to fear any talk of prajna. Believing and understanding they have not yet, to say nothing of receiving and upholding. How then could they together ascend the road of awakening and not be blocked at the conjured city? Hence he points out one by one the reason why they cannot believe, understand, receive, and uphold, so that all who hear may know that dharmas are from the first without fixed nature and that the Buddha does not deceive people. Why be startled, terrified, doubtful, or afraid? Thus there may be hope that they will believe, understand, receive, and uphold. Hence the words below about the first paramita precisely make clear that dharmas have no fixed mark; and the words about the five discourses precisely make clear that the Buddha does not deceive people. It can be seen that the present words, "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid," are precisely the groundwork for what is said below. And the intent of speaking what is below is precisely to cut off the startlement, terror, doubt, and fear of beings. The sense of the words before and after closely answers each other.

To say "most" of what is rare is also the meaning of "foremost and most rare." Judging by the tone of "if again there are" and what follows, it is also confirming what the elder said. The words above, "so it is, so it is," have already confirmed and settled it. That he speaks these few further words has no other purpose than to set forth the root of the disease in those beings who cannot believe, understand, receive, and uphold, so as to encourage them.

(Gui) 2. Unfolding the meaning. In two parts: (Zi) 1. Unfolding the meaning that contemplation and practice are free from marks; 2. Unfolding the true meaning of Dharma-speaking. (Zi) 1. Again in two: (Chou) 1. Making it clear by way of prajna; 2. Making it clear by way of the remaining paramitas.
(Chou) 1. Making it clear by way of prajna.
["Why? Subhuti, what the Tathagata says is the first paramita is not the first paramita; therefore it is named the first paramita."]

The words "why?" govern the whole section on patience below. In "first paramita," the two words "first" refer to prajna. "What the Tathagata says" shows that it is spoken by way of the nature. Spoken by way of the nature, it is therefore said to be first and not first. For the nature-substance is empty and still; how could there be such a mark as this first paramita? Hence it says "not." To say "not" makes clear that its nature is from the first no mark, and therefore one should not grasp at marks. And again, spoken by way of the nature, it says it is named the first paramita. For though the nature-substance has no mark, it is also not without marks. All marks arise in dependence on the nature; this first paramita too arises in dependence on the nature, and is not without the name and mark of "first"; hence it says "is named." To say "is named" makes clear that its mark is not apart from the nature, and that one should still return and merge it into the nature.

Spoken thus, this is the basic meaning of this section's text. It is called the basic meaning because wherever this sutra says "not" or "is named," it is illuminating this meaning. This is the fundamental meaning, which students may not fail to understand. Yet the meaning of this section is exceedingly profound and exceedingly important. Were one to speak only this basic meaning, it would not be the Buddha's intent. For everything from this section onward unfolds the meaning, and to unfold the meaning is to bring out, beyond the basic meaning, further meanings that are deduced and illuminated. What are they? Consider that he opens his mouth with "Why?" These three words come in continuation of the words above: "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid; you should know that such persons are most rare." It can be known that the three lines on the first paramita precisely explain why one is not startled, and so on, and why such a one is rare. If one spoke only the basic meaning and did not bring out clearly the reason within it, then the three words "why?" and the words above about not being startled and so on would have no place to rest. Above it says "you should know"; this is precisely what students should know and must not fail to understand deeply. Not only this. Above it does not say "believe, understand, receive, and uphold," but changes the wording to "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid," because beings of the final age have the disease of fearing any talk of prajna and being unable to believe, understand, receive, and uphold. Here it does not say "prajna-paramita" but changes the wording to "the first paramita," thereby using it to unfold and bring out the essential principle of prajna, so that all beings may understand it clearly. Thus they may suddenly realize that prajna need not be feared and cannot be feared, and only then can they be counted as people who study the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi and only then have they hope of turning the ordinary into the sage. Why? Was it not said above that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra? That is to say plainly that prajna absolutely must be believed, understood, received, and upheld, and that one should enter by this gate. If one does not enter by this sutra's gate, one cuts oneself off from the Dharma of unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment, and cuts oneself off from all Buddhas as well. Why? Since all Buddhas and the unsurpassed Dharma all come forth from this sutra, one who wishes to study the unsurpassed Dharma and to turn the ordinary into the sage, if he does not enter by this sutra, does he not cut off his own road? How could it be something to be feared? Therefore if one speaks only the basic meaning, only the former layer of meaning, and does not bring out thoroughly such profound meaning, then the World-Honored One's profound intent in changing the wording would be buried. Above it says "you should know"; this is what students especially should know and absolutely must understand deeply. All the various reasons above are contained within these three lines of text; one may imagine how extraordinarily profound their meaning is, and how important their bearing is.

To explain them, one must skillfully devise expedients, so that the words are few and the meaning clear. One should know that the meaning of prajna has lain hidden and obscure for a thousand ages. Now if one wishes to remove the disease of fearing it, one cannot but expose the cause of that fear. Sometimes one cannot avoid touching on the ancients, and cannot keep silent out of regard for the worthy. For if the hidden and obscure meaning is not thoroughly explained, the root of the disease of startlement, doubt, terror, and fear remains, and one still cannot believe or understand, and is unwilling to receive and uphold; would that not be to fail the Buddha's kindness? I deeply hope you will all quiet your minds and listen attentively. If this meaning is not thoroughly understood, it will likewise be to have failed the Buddha's kindness.

Since the principle is so profound and subtle, though I now wish for few words and clear meaning, a few sentences cannot possibly make it clear, nor can it be grasped in a single breath. I will first take the two words "first" and set forth a rough outline, so that the listeners may have a foundation in their minds; then step by step we will go deeper. This too is the sense of an expedient.

Prajna-paramita is called the first paramita because prajna is the mother of the paramitas. If prajna is the mother, the paramitas are the children, and children cannot be apart from their mother. Hence one who practices the paramitas, if he lacks the practice of prajna, cannot, as to cause, break delusion, and as to fruition, can hardly realize the dharma-body. One should know that the paramitas are all called paramitas precisely because prajna is within them; without prajna they cannot be called paramitas. Why? Because otherwise they cannot break delusion, cannot realize the dharma-body, and cannot reach the other shore. This is why prajna has the name of the first paramita. From this one sees that since the paramitas cannot be apart from prajna, prajna likewise does not exist apart from the paramitas; this can be known. Hence the second line says, "is not the first paramita." This one word "not" makes clear that one must not grasp prajna as having a separate mark. Yet though it is not separate, it is not without the name "first"; hence the third line says, "is named the first paramita." These two words "is named" make clear that while the paramitas apart from prajna are not paramitas, prajna is not without the mere name of leader. The above explains why prajna is named first, and also explains why, spoken by way of "first," it is said to be "not" and "is named." This meaning must be firmly remembered; it is the ground for breaking people's startlement, doubt, terror, and fear. What follows will speak of it.

Above, the elder used the fact that the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark to make clear that such a person's emptiness and existence are perfectly fused, and thereby to explain why he is foremost and most rare. The World-Honored One has already confirmed and approved it. But whenever the World-Honored One speaks a dharma, it is never for one affair alone, never for one person alone. So because of this person's rarity he perceived that the reason all beings have the mark of self is nothing else: they grasp at dharmas. Hence after confirming and approving, he further unfolds the meaning by way of the six paramitas and other dharmas, to instruct all beings who discriminate and grasp at dharmas. That he speaks of prajna first is precisely because beings fear prajna. Why do beings fear it? Because they discriminate and grasp at dharmas, and do not understand the true meaning of prajna. This is why he unfolds it for them. For when beings suddenly hear that prajna is the emptiness of the supreme meaning, they think it lofty and hard to practice, and so are startled. And not understanding why the emptiness of the supreme meaning is so, they are terrified. Feeling that instead of studying prajna they had better study some other perfect sutra and perfect dharma that is safer, they are afraid. All this comes from not having penetrated the Buddha's principle, so that they mistakenly give rise to the grasping at dharmas through discrimination. This is truly to lose one's own good benefit, and is deeply pitiable. Hence the World-Honored One, explaining why such a person is most rare, says: why do I call such a person most rare? Because in this prajna Dharma-gate beings are startled, doubtful, terrified, and afraid, and this person alone is not.

This dharma is indeed lofty, so why wonder that they are startled and afraid? Yet this dharma is most essential; how can one obstruct oneself? I will now further unfold for the great assembly the true meaning of prajna, which among the paramitas is called first, so that they may understand it clearly. I speak of prajna in order to lead beings to the other shore. Not to reach the other shore is to sink in the sea of suffering, and without prajna one cannot reach the other shore. It can be seen that this dharma is exceedingly important, that one absolutely must not doubt, fear, and obstruct oneself, and that one must believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. What is the other shore? It is the true mark of all dharmas. One should know that the true mark is no mark. Hence prajna, though called first, is not first. Why? Because "first" is from the first without mark. Since it is from the first without fixed mark, it is said to be "not." To say "not" is to make beings understand clearly that of the dharmas the Buddha speaks, there is not one dharma that can be apart from prajna; so prajna cannot vaunt itself as first apart from the paramitas. Again one should know that the true mark is also not without marks. Hence prajna, though not first, is named first. Why? Because "first" is not without a mere name. Since it is not without the name and mark of a mere existence, it says "is named." To say "is named" is to make beings understand clearly that since every dharma is not apart from prajna, every dharma may be named first; so prajna's being called first is a mere name.

I have thus unfolded the essential meaning of prajna, and all beings should be able to awaken to it through this. Wherever I say "not," it is certainly to make people empty marks; and then I say "is named," to show that it is not without the name and mark of a mere existence. So what is called emptying marks is to empty the disease of grasping at marks, and is not to destroy the marks. This can be clearly understood. Not destroying the marks is to empty even the emptiness that is one-sidedly grasped; this is what is called the emptiness of the supreme meaning. If one can penetrate this meaning, one knows that because marks are mere names they must not be grasped, not that there are no marks; and that because dharmas have no fixed nature they must not be grasped, not that there are no dharmas. Then though this dharma is empty, how could it be the same as a blank, stubborn emptiness? And though this dharma is lofty, it is not without a place to begin. What then is there to be startled at, terrified of, or afraid of? Now such a person can believe, understand, receive, and uphold, and so is neither startled nor terrified nor afraid. He has penetrated the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and is precisely what is called one whose mind is not startled or moved with respect to the supreme meaning. Is he not most rare? What has been said above not only explains why the earlier text says "neither startled" and so on up to "most rare," but also thoroughly explains the principle that all beings need not fear and must not fear, so that the meaning of this section is fully brought out.

Yet there remains an essential meaning that cannot but be spoken. What is it? It is what was said above to have lain hidden and obscure for a thousand ages. One should know that the disease of fearing prajna is deep and long-standing. If one does not expose its causes one by one, how can one remove the thousand-year disease of preconceptions? All the more should one explain in detail that the meaning of prajna is perfectly fused, in no way different from what is called the middle way and the supreme meaning, and has nothing whatever to be feared. Thus one may not lose one's own good benefit. Though this is said by way of extension, it is still the purport of this section's text; the intent is to break the grasping at dharmas through discrimination and so remove the root of the disease of fearing any talk of prajna.

The sutras say that the two vehicles fear emptiness, which means they fear the emptiness of the supreme meaning of prajna. It can be seen that this was already so in the Buddha's time, and not only in later ages. But in the Buddha's time only the two vehicles gave rise to fear; the Great Vehicle did not yet have this disease. Later, when Xuanzang crossed to the west and met the masters of the Yogacara school in that land, he set the emptiness of the nature school over against the existence of the mark school. (The emptiness of the supreme meaning is absolute emptiness; how could it be set over against existence?) Once this point was mistaken, it was said that the mark school alone is the definitive meaning; this is the so-called classification of the teachings into three periods. Thus even among the Mahayana people of India at that time, there were already those who could not deeply understand the meaning and who mistook prajna for one-sided emptiness. As for those in our Sui and Tang dynasties who classified the teachings, they likewise never placed prajna among the perfect teachings. They were not unaware that it is the emptiness of the supreme meaning, but in the end they thought that since it speaks exclusively of emptiness it is not as perfectly fused as the middle way and the supreme meaning. That the ancients judged it so was meant to exalt what they themselves followed, and they could not but deliberately show a bias. Yet the bias went too far, and they inevitably grasped at the mark of words. Later people, because it was so judged by the ancients, grasped all the more and were all the more overawed at the sight of it. Hence never has anyone been willing to study prajna or willing to speak of prajna. This is truly sad, truly lamentable.

The Chan school, though it takes prajna as its guiding principle, takes only its sweeping-away flavor for its practice and does not speak of the teaching. So the meaning of prajna has not been made clear for a thousand ages. In the Chen and Sui dynasties there was the Three Treatise school, but it took the treatises as its guiding principle, not the sutra. What the three treatises make clear is certainly prajna, but since the masters of the three treatises devoted themselves to researching the words of the treatises, they could not avoid being out of touch with the meaning of the sutra. Why? Because they had not directly contemplated it. In plain terms, they still could not avoid grasping at the mark of the three treatises' words. Hence the masters of the three treatises expounded the meaning of the treatises most exquisitely, yet the purport of the sutra they could not touch at the itchy place. One should know that since prajna is the mother of the paramitas, and this sutra plainly says that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment come forth from this sutra, then if the meaning of prajna is not clear, even reading other perfectly fused sutras and treatises, one has not worked at the fundamental meaning, and how could one's insight be thorough? And if the insight is not thorough, how could it be perfect? Now the World-Honored One, taking the name of the first paramita, unfolds its meaning, so that one may know that the meaning of prajna is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty, and perfectly fused, thereby keeping beings from being startled, terrified, doubtful, and afraid, from losing the treasure of the Dharma through neglect, and from finding it hard to reach the other shore. It is as though he foresaw where the root of the disease of fear would lie in later people and set it before them in advance; truly great kindness and great compassion.

Above, whenever I have spoken of "is not" and "is named," I have mostly explained them by way of non-grasping at the two extremes, that is, by way of the perfectly fused middle way. This time I explain them also by way of the emptiness of the supreme meaning, that is, by way of sweeping away. To speak thus truly involves pains. What pains? To make one know that the middle way and sweeping away, though the words differ, are in meaning truly without difference. How is this shown? It is named the emptiness of the supreme meaning because it empties through to the very bottom. Emptying through to the very bottom means that existence too is emptied and emptiness too is emptied. In other words, existence is relinquished and emptiness is relinquished. Relinquishing existence is what is called not grasping at existence; relinquishing emptiness, is that not what is called not grasping at emptiness? Then between the sweeping-away emptiness of the supreme meaning and the perfectly fused middle way of non-grasping at the two extremes, pray what difference is there? From this one may know that what the classifiers of the teachings said cannot be held as a settled verdict; this can now be clearly understood. And those who fear any talk of prajna may well turn about and repent. Moreover, from this it follows that all the sayings that some sutra is purely perfect and some sutra is not purely perfect likewise cannot be held as fixed marks. Why? Since every dharma is prajna, every dharma is perfect. As is said, when a perfect person speaks the Dharma, no dharma is not perfect. Why insist on discriminating?

It was said above that sweeping away and the perfectly fused middle way are without the slightest difference. Those who mistakenly believe there is a difference have no other reason than that they stare fixedly at the middle way. I will now further unfold its meaning by way of the middle way, so that it may be thoroughly understood, and then the grasping of discrimination may perhaps not arise of itself.

Since all dharmas are mere names, the middle way too is a mere name. Being a mere name, it has no fixed mark and therefore must not be grasped; to grasp it is to fall into the four marks, and can that still be called the perfectly fused middle way? One should know that the one word "middle" comes into being through contrast with the two extremes. If one leaves the two extremes, the middle is nowhere to be found. Hence the middle has no fixed mark. And marks being without fixity, how can one stare fixedly at it? To stare fixedly is to fall into grasping at dharmas. One should further know that the reason the middle has no fixed mark is that the two extremes are likewise mere names, likewise arising through contrast, and likewise from the first without fixed mark. Since the two extremes must not be grasped, how could there be a middle to grasp? Hence one who truly understands the meaning of the middle finds no place that is not the middle: even emptiness and the mere name are both the middle.

Take emptiness as an illustration. Emptiness means not grasping at existence; and when emptiness itself is also emptied, that is not grasping at emptiness. So emptying through to the very bottom returns to the middle way, as was made clear above. For this reason prajna and the Avatamsaka and Lotus sutras are in meaning without difference. Not only this: carrying the mere name through to the very bottom is likewise so. For example, to know that all dharmas are not without a mere name is not to grasp at emptiness; and to further know that the name is merely provisional, is that not not grasping at existence? Then it too is plainly the middle way. This is why the Mantra and Pure Land schools both enter the Way through the gate of existence and both are perfect and sudden great dharmas. Even of the mark school one may say that it is from the first the perfect meaning of the Great Vehicle. Not to speak of other matters, consider how it unfolds the principle of the three natures, the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected; how perfect and wondrous. Yet alas, those who study it do not contemplate and work at these places but devote themselves to analyzing trivial names and marks. The more they analyze, the more they discriminate, and so the more they grasp. Thus the great becomes small and the perfect becomes one-sided; they may be called poor students. Not knowing how to use it to remove ordinary feeling, they instead increase ordinary feeling through it. How could this be the original intent of the Buddha's speaking of dharma-marks? Those who cultivate the Mantra and Pure Land schools, if they do not understand the meaning that self and other are non-dual and mind and land are non-dual, likewise make the great small and the perfect one-sided. From this one may know that whatever the Buddha spoke is from the first perfect in every dharma, and that where people see it as not perfect, it is truly due to the one-sided views of beings and has nothing to do with the Dharma. Hence one who studies Buddhism must first open wide a perfect understanding, contemplating the principle that there is no place that is not the middle, and cultivating all dharmas thereby; then every dharma is perfect, every dharma is the middle way and the supreme meaning, every dharma is the first paramita, and every dharma realizes the true mark and reaches the other shore. This is what is called the perfect middle, which students absolutely must know.

The four words just spoken, "open wide a perfect understanding," deserve the closest attention. All my sayings that there is no place that is not the middle can only be a small aid to the hearer. One must constantly take this perfect meaning and, upon one's own mind and upon all dharmas, subtly and closely contemplate it and work at it with vigor, so as to remove the one-sided and grasping ordinary feeling; only then may one's own perfect understanding perhaps be opened. Otherwise what is called perfect understanding still belongs to someone else and is not one's own. Though one knows that no place is not the middle, with respect to all dharmas one will still meet obstruction at every turn and cannot be without a place that is not the middle. This point is of the utmost importance; do not neglect it by any means. Not only is this one meaning so; all the meanings spoken are so. In short, hearing, reflection, and cultivation cannot be lacking in any one.

One should further know that this sutra's speaking of "is not" and "is named" makes clear that nature and mark are neither one nor different: though perfectly fused, they are laid out in order, and though laid out in order, they are perfectly fused. ("Laid out in order" is the sense of "thus, thus," that is, one yet two. "Perfectly fused" is two yet one. The above showed that sweeping away is the middle way, making clear that it is the same in meaning as the Lotus Sutra; here it shows that it is the same in meaning as the Avatamsaka.) Why? Wherever it says "is not," it speaks by way of the nature; spoken by way of the nature, one should not grasp at marks, and so it says "not." That one should not grasp at marks and so says "not" makes clear that nature and mark are not one. Wherever it says "is named," it speaks by way of marks; spoken by way of marks, one should not destroy marks, and so it affirms them. That one should not destroy marks and so affirms them makes clear that nature and mark are not different. Why? The nature is substance and marks are function, utterly distinct, and so they are not one; this is what is called being laid out in order. Yet function is born from substance, and apart from substance there is no function; from this one may know that marks are the working of the nature. Understanding this principle and not grasping, one sees the nature in seeing marks, and so they are not different; this is what is called perfect fusion. Since nature and mark are thus neither one nor different, it is one yet two, two yet one. Being one yet two, one should neither destroy nor grasp them; for though they are not different, they are already not one, and so one must see the laid-out order within the perfect fusion and obtain the perfect fusion within the laid-out order. Being two yet one, though marks blaze forth, they still return and merge into the nature; for though they are not one they are truly not different, and so one should let the perfect fusion not obstruct the laid-out order, nor the laid-out order the perfect fusion. In thus unfolding it, I find it plainly no different in meaning from the Avatamsaka, and those who follow the Avatamsaka need not fear. And as was said above, sweeping away and the middle way are without difference; if one understands this meaning, those who follow the Lotus Sutra need not fear either.

In this sutra, passages such as "if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata," "one should produce a pure mind," "one should produce the mind without dwelling," as well as the two words "true mark," and "the mark of self is precisely non-mark" and so on here, can all be explained by this meaning. Even when the sutra opens and speaks of various kinds of beings and of nirvana without residue, that too is perfect fusion within the laid-out order. And when it further says that in truth there is no being who is ferried into extinction, then the laid-out order is perfectly fused. Here I have merely taken "is not" and "is named" and unfolded them thus, so that those who follow the Avatamsaka need not look askance at it. If one insists that only "is not" and "is named" can make this meaning clear, that again is wrong. In short, grasp the essential and comprehend the whole, and there is no saying that will not do. From this one may awaken to the fact that dharmas have no fixed mark.

There is a further most essential meaning that must be spoken. Since the sweeping-away Dharma-gate and the perfect-fusion Dharma-gate are without the slightest difference, why was it said above that one must enter by this sutra? One should know that though these two Dharma-gates are without difference in principle, in practice they differ greatly in sharpness and dullness. The reason one should enter by this sutra is that all ordinary beings without exception are deeply diseased with one-sided grasping, and must sweep away with all one's might before one can be perfectly fused. Otherwise, with not a fraction of the ordinary feeling of one-sided grasping removed, how could one comprehend a perfectly fused sutra or treatise, and how could one benefit from it? At most one might learn a doctrine or two to assist in idle talk.

Consider how since the Tang dynasty, among the great masters outside the Chan school, those whose virtue and insight later generations most admire, when one examines where they gained their strength, were almost all without exception tempered in the Chan gate. This is precisely because the practice of the Chan gate takes as its guiding principle prajna's emptiness of emptiness and sweeps away the one-sided grasping of students with all its might. Hence I have often said that after the Tang, Chinese Buddhism depended entirely on the Chan school. From this one may know the importance of the work of sweeping away, and that the meaning of prajna's three emptinesses must be understood. But when sweeping away, one should deeply and perfectly contemplate the perfectly fused meaning of the sutra. Otherwise one will not know what is one-sided, what is grasping, and what should be swept away; one may even think one is sweeping away when in fact one is only increasing one-sided grasping. This is why the Chan gate, though it does not speak of doctrine, must have strict and clear-eyed teachers and companions who constantly wield the tongs and hammer on one's behalf. What is called wielding the tongs and hammer is sweeping away and sweeping away again; what is called the hundred-foot pole requiring one further step.

Now since one has not met strict and clear-eyed teachers and companions, one can only observe and illuminate oneself, closely and precisely comprehending the sutra's clarifications of non-grasping at the two extremes and the perfect fusion of nature and mark. Or it speaks of emptying through to the very bottom, and even, the more it speaks, the deeper it goes, as in the latter half: all dharmas are one suchness, everything is, no sage and no ordinary being, from the first no arising, and so on. The student should assess how much his own level can bear, and from the shallow to the deep take up one phrase or join several phrases and use them to contemplate his own mind. If his own habitual tendencies, and even the arising of a single thought, are the least bit out of accord with the sutra's intent, that is one-sided grasping; then he should at once strike and shout at himself and sweep it away. This is the most wondrous method of practice, truly the talk of my own experience, which I make bold to tell you all.

Other perfectly fused sutras and teachings, if one enjoys studying them, may be looked at as well, but one should take prajna as the master. Why? The Avatamsaka, Lotus, and the like are expressive statements; an expressive statement uses language that displays perfect fusion in order to make clear the nature-substance. Hence their phrases and flavor all tend toward perfect fusion; even when they speak of the method of sweeping away, it is lodged within the perfect fusion. So only one who already has the work of sweeping away, that is, one whose grasping views are already thin, can thoroughly comprehend them. Otherwise one knows only that they speak of perfect fusion and does not know that they speak of sweeping away. Hence those who enter by them often study for many years while the disease of one-sided grasping remains. They may expound perfect fusion according to the doctrine, yet it has no bearing on their own portion. Moreover, with the grasping feeling unsubdued, what they say is no more than a surface show; sometimes it looks profound and subtle, but examined closely it is neither clear nor awake. Or they think that only such-and-such a sutra is so and others are not, and still they do not see that they can truly be perfectly fused. Prajna, however, is a negating statement; a negating statement uses language that sweeps away one-sided grasping in order to make clear the nature-substance. Hence its phrases and flavor all tend toward sweeping away; even when it speaks of the principle of perfect fusion, that is lodged within the sweeping away. This is why people fear any talk of prajna, and also why prajna is not placed among the perfect teachings: because they look at only one side of the words. On this one point alone it can be proved that one who has not worked at prajna, even though he studies other perfect sutras, still has an insight that is kept apart and not perfectly fused.

The above has spoken of how prajna differs in its formulation from other perfect sutras, and of the subtle point on which the sharpness or dullness of those who study it depends. Now, to uphold the true Dharma and to let everyone obtain benefit, I have not shrunk from turning it over and over in full detail and laying it out thread by thread for you all. From this one may know the wonder of prajna, and that one must study it first. Why? For every portion of grasping feeling that is swept away, nature and mark are perfectly fused by one portion; sweeping away carried to its utmost is perfect fusion carried to its utmost. Wisdom penetrating the three emptinesses is the perfectly fused middle way. How wondrous, how wondrous! This is enough to show that prajna is not only the broad highway of studying Buddhism but its direct path. If one does not enter by this gate, does one not fail to know the way? This is why many study Buddhism and few attain freedom. All that I have said here is one word, one drop of blood, all gained through a thousand hardships; all is my heart and liver dug out and shown to others. And these sutra passages unfolding the meaning are one word, one pearl, utterly perfect and utterly round. You must truly and earnestly comprehend them and not neglect them.

I said just now that after the Tang dynasty Chinese Buddhism depended entirely on the Chan school. Do not misunderstand this as urging people not to recite the Buddha's name and to go practice Chan instead. For where I praise the Chan school, I am praising prajna; I am urging people to study prajna, not urging them to practice Chan. One should know that to practice Chan one must weigh the time and the capacity. Capacity is capacity and time is time; they are not one thing. What is called capacity means one's own faculties. So one should first ask whether one can take a blow and a shout. Whether one's faculties are sharp or dull matters less; unless one has the spirit of a death-defying band, there is no use speaking of it. Again, capacity also means opportunity. So one should further ask whether one has met a good teacher. Chan practice cannot be apart from a teacher, and the teacher must not only be clear but fierce, and must further have the means to kill and to give life. Lacking any of the three, he is not a good teacher. If both one's faculties and one's opportunity are complete, Chan practice is very good. If either is lacking, to speak of practicing Chan will bring no benefit and may bring harm. This too is my talk of experience. What is called time: in the Northern and Southern Dynasties, Northern Wei and Southern Liang both greatly promoted the Buddha Dharma, and lecture seats were at their height; yet they could not avoid grasping at the mark of words. Hence when Bodhidharma came east he set up no words and pointed directly at the mind, precisely to meet the disease of the time. Today most people do not understand the Buddha's principle, so one should broadly encourage the reading of sutras to cure their emptiness and shallowness. To set up no words is still not fitting today. So it is better to arouse the great compassionate vow, cultivate merit and keep the precepts, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and draw near to the two great good teachers Sakyamuni and Amitabha. On the one hand, relying on what I have said above, use this sutra's principle to contemplate one's own mind and sweep away its ordinary feeling; on the other hand, earnestly hold the name, seeking to be reborn in the Pure Land together with all beings and to fulfill the bodhi vow. For practice in this present life there is nothing that surpasses this method. This is what I, unwise as I am, have earnestly practiced these near twenty years, and I respectfully offer it to all good teachers. Again, since I began lecturing I have spoken of many methods of practice. Do not insist on which is the best; choose the one you are good at and practice it. Or try each one in turn, and whichever you find effective is the one best suited to your capacity. This too is the key to practice, and I tell it to you all.

The great reason for fearing any talk of prajna, spoken of above, is that people have neither understood the sutra's meaning nor been free of preconceived words, so that they grow the more terrified and the less willing to study. Yet there is another great reason which one must also know: the great number of those who talk wildly of prajna. The disease of wild talk existed in ancient times and is still more virulent today. Such people, though they have studied Buddhism, have very heavy former karma and do not understand the Buddha Dharma. Suddenly, as if gone mad, they break the precepts utterly, show no respect for the Three Jewels, and give free rein to evil. They practice greed, anger, and delusion in earnest and take themselves to be practicing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, saying that this is prajna's non-grasping at marks. Thereupon those who fear prajna seize it as a pretext and warn one another not to dare to utter a single word of prajna, until it is almost a matter of turning pale at the mention of a tiger. Alas, to give up eating because of a choking fit, what a perverse plan. One should know that since there is this grotesque wild talk, one should all the more arouse the mind to study it and to spread it, and only then can the true meaning of prajna be fully made clear. When the true meaning is clear, whence would the grotesque wild talk arise? Not knowing to do this, but only shutting the door and stubbornly refusing, one's disease, though different in appearance from that of the wild talker, has the same root; for both mistakenly take prajna for one-sided emptiness. Judged by cause and effect, the guilt of wild talk is indeed heavy, but except for the retinue of demons, people can know it and keep away from it. The fearer of talk, however, is taken by people as a standard and they do not even know he is mistaken, so that prajna, which surpasses all dharmas and on which the life-breath of the Buddha Dharma depends, is left unheeded by anyone. I fear the evil fruit summoned by his evil cause of harming the Dharma and harming people may not be much lighter.

Our World-Honored One clearly knew the diseases of all beings, so the earlier words that one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit can give rise to faith and take this as real were a sharp lancet for those who talk wildly; and these several sections now are again a sharp lancet for those who fear to talk. Looking at what was said before, it shuts the wild talkers outside the gate. Why? Faith is the gate of entry to the path. Since it is by keeping the precepts and cultivating merit that one enters the gate, the wild talker who breaks the precepts and commits offenses is decisively shut outside. Looking at what these several sections say, they again warn the fearer of talk that he can by no means turn the ordinary into the sage. Why? Only one who is neither startled nor terrified nor afraid is allowed to be rare, so the fearer of talk clearly remains an ordinary, foolish being. And above it says "take this as real," while here it unfolds the meaning; this is plainly to instruct that if one wishes to remove the diseases of wild talk and fearful talk, there is nothing but believing, understanding, receiving, and upholding, and earnestly seeking to understand the true meaning within the sutra. Again, the fearful have a constant saying: Do I not know that prajna should be studied? Truly, beings of the final age have deep obstacles and heavy karma and cannot easily attain it; better not to speak of it and so avoid adding to one's offenses. This again is a mistake. Did the World-Honored One not plainly say: after the Tathagata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, who can give rise to faith, take this as real, and even obtain immeasurable merit and virtue? So to call them rare in the final age is fine, but to conclude that there are absolutely none, and to warn one another and block the road, is not only to slight beings but plainly to disobey the Buddha's intent. The World-Honored One's admonition to the elder not to speak thus is no different from admonishing the fearer of talk not to speak thus. And in these several sections the Buddha and the elder both encourage and exhort later ages specifically; all of it foresees the excessive worries of the fearful and instructs them, and is truly intimate and savory.

Again, in citing the name of the first paramita here, and in saying "not" and "is named," there is a further meaning that must be made clear. The one name "prajna" is easily misunderstood as referring to the single paramita of prajna alone, whereas the name "first" was from the first established to show that it penetrates the other five paramitas. Explaining the meaning on this basis makes it hard to grasp and easy to understand. Moreover, to say that the first is not first makes still clearer the meaning that all the paramitas are one prajna and that prajna does not exist apart from the paramitas. As for saying "is named": since none of the paramitas is other than prajna, how could the title "first" belong to prajna alone? Since it is not its alone, then though it is so it is a mere name; this makes clear that one must not grasp it as existent. And because of prajna's being first, every paramita becomes first; so though it is a mere name, it is very much so; this makes clear that one must not grasp it as non-existent. In sum, it makes clear only that prajna and the paramitas cannot be apart from each other. Hence this section unfolds the meaning by way of prajna and the next section again unfolds it by way of the other paramitas. Such is the skill of Dharma-speaking; such is the thoroughness with which the meaning is made clear.

As to the essential meanings in this section's text, let me now gather the most essential and reduce them to a few phrases for ease of memory.
