They are: the most essential meaning of this section is to cure the disease of those who fear prajna. The disease has two forms: first, fearing emptiness; second, fearing loftiness. Now it is made clear that prajna does not exist apart from the other five paramitas, and that the other paramitas are all gates of practice; it can be seen that though prajna makes clear the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of emptiness cannot be apart from actual practice, and it is clear that prajna is by no means one-sided emptiness. Why then fear it? It is further made clear that the other paramitas apart from prajna are not paramitas; in plain terms, they cannot reach the other shore. It can be seen that prajna is indeed lofty, yet it must be studied; and it is clear how important its bearing is. Why then fear it? This is the utmost of warning; keep it in mind and do not forget it.
(Chou) 2. Making it clear by way of the remaining paramitas. In two parts: (Yin) 1. Directly making it clear; 2. Citing proof.
(Yin) 1. Directly making it clear.
["Subhuti, what the Tathagata says is the paramita of patience is not the paramita of patience."]

The remaining paramitas are, apart from prajna, the other five of giving, keeping the precepts, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration. Every dharma should be free from marks, and so no dharma can be apart from prajna. That among the remaining five he singles out patience alone is because patience is the hardest to free from marks, and its inability to be apart from prajna is the easier to comprehend. Hence he specially cites this paramita to unfold its meaning, thereby covering the others. So the section heading does not say "patience" but "the remaining paramitas," precisely because the Buddha's speaking of it was meant to let beings infer the three corners from one. Such a heading follows what the Buddha said, relying on the meaning and not on the words.

The above, making it clear by way of prajna, unfolded from the front side the true meaning of freedom from marks. For people know only that prajna speaks of emptiness and freedom from marks, and those who grasp at marks therefore give rise to fear. Now it is made clear that even the mark of prajna should be relinquished, which is to relinquish emptiness as well. Moreover, prajna is within the other five paramitas and cannot stand alone, and the other five paramitas are all dharmas of actual practice; so what is called freedom from marks is the relinquishing of the mark of dharma and the mark of non-dharma together. If one understands this meaning, one may boldly study prajna; why fear it?

This making it clear by way of patience unfolds from the reverse side the true meaning that one cannot but be free from marks. Looking at what is said below: if one practices the dharma of patience and is not free from the mark of patience, one gives rise to hatred, and hatred is precisely the opposite of patience. This makes clear that one who practices the dharma of patience, if he does not study prajna, does not know to be free from the mark of the dharma of patience; not being free from the mark of dharma, hatred arises; and once hatred arises, the merit of patience is destroyed and it becomes the mark of non-dharma. From this one may awaken to the fact that the reason one must be free from the mark of dharma is precisely to be free from the mark of non-dharma. How wondrous, how wondrous. If one understands this meaning, one will surely apply the mind to studying prajna and cannot fear it. Unfolded thus, the essential meaning of prajna is exposed to the very bottom, and one may clearly see that prajna absolutely must be studied.

These several sections of sutra text unfolding the meaning have expounded the principle of prajna and the principle that prajna should be studied with the utmost subtlety, perfection, penetration, and fineness. You should earnestly quiet your minds and comprehend them; for every portion comprehended is a portion of benefit obtained. Moreover, these several sections are precisely the crystallization of all the meanings spoken above. If the meaning here can be clearly penetrated, then all the meanings above will shine clear in your breast one by one.

That this section follows immediately upon the last carries a further sense. The intent is to use patience's inability to be apart from prajna to prove and complete the last section's meaning that prajna does not exist apart from the other paramitas. For since all the remaining paramitas must have prajna, it can be seen that prajna is a dharma that goes along with the remaining paramitas and is not a dharma practiced separately. In short, prajna is the mother of the paramitas, and the paramitas are the children of prajna. If there were no children, the name mother could not stand; if there were no mother, the name children could not stand. Mother and children truly complete each other. So prajna and the remaining paramitas must complete each other; how could they be apart? Prajna is emptiness; the remaining paramitas are existence. To say now that prajna and the other five paramitas cannot be apart is to make students comprehend that emptiness and existence are from the first simultaneous, and so cannot be apart.

Because emptiness and existence are simultaneous, one should not grasp at the two extremes but return and merge into the middle way. There is a further point. Speaking in terms of mother and children, they certainly should complete each other; yet the children are truly born from the mother, and without the mother there are no children. So within their mutual help, the mother should still be the master. The six paramitas are likewise: the other five paramitas without prajna are not paramitas. So the other five paramitas truly arise from the first paramita, and within their mutual help prajna is still the master. To take prajna as master is to take emptiness as master. Taking emptiness as master, though one should not destroy existence, one still should not grasp at existence; and though one returns and merges into the middle way, one does not grasp at the middle either. This is why the Buddhas and bodhisattvas take the great emptiness-samadhi as ultimate, and take no wisdom and no attainment as the attainment of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment. For only thus can one follow forms through the six paths and manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies, while though all dharmas blaze forth, the one mind is limpid and from the first nothing is produced. This is what is called great freedom; this is what is called great benefit. It is on this alone that one can ferry all suffering and distress. This is the ultimate meaning of prajna, and the latter half of the sutra precisely makes it clear. Taking this occasion to disclose a hint of it shows that prajna is the meaning in the Buddha Dharma that runs from beginning to end: without studying it one cannot enter the gate, and without studying it one cannot reach the ultimate. Why then fear it?

And from this one may know that to speak exclusively of non-grasping at the two extremes and the perfectly fused middle way is still not the ultimate meaning of the Buddha Dharma. Why? Without emptiness upon emptiness, there is sure to be something grasped. Not grasping at the extremes, one is sure to grasp at the middle; where then is the perfect fusion? Moreover, in the great emptiness-samadhi even the two words "perfect fusion" are unattainable. One should know that only when it is unattainable is perfect fusion attained. Why? Not grasping at perfect fusion, one attains perfect fusion. With the slightest mark, it is neither round nor fused. Then since the meaning of prajna is ultimate in this way, how could it be only the first gate of entry to the path? Why classify it as the initial teaching of the Great Vehicle? And prajna runs through all the paramitas, and the paramitas apart from it are not paramitas; so it can be seen that if there is a single dharma apart from it, one cannot be complete. Thus the meaning of prajna is the utmost of completeness and surpasses all Dharma-gates; this too can be known. Why then not allow it to be purely perfect, but classify it as separate and also perfect?

The above spoke of the six paramitas helping one another; there is a further essential meaning that must be known. Prajna is principle, is wisdom, what is called the gate of contemplation. The paramitas are affairs, are objects, what is called the gate of practice. That after speaking of the first paramita he further speaks of the remaining paramitas is to make clear that principle and affairs have never been apart, that contemplation and practice should advance together, and that object and wisdom above all must be merged in pairs. So judging by the text it seems to start a separate topic, but examining the meaning it is truly one thread. The textual surface of this sutra is for the most part like this; what is called the text not joining but the meaning joining. To regard them as having nothing to do with each other would be a great mistake.

The circulating editions have the line "is named the paramita of patience." This was added by someone between the Ming and Qing, and appears in the Sun family edition of the Qianlong-Jiaqing period. Its note says: "The ancients did not have this line, but by principle it should be there." They did not realize that the words "not" here are precisely the groundwork for the text below, which makes clear that if patience is not free from marks the Dharma-gate of patience is utterly destroyed, thereby revealing that it absolutely cannot be apart from prajna. If one suddenly adds a line "is named," blocking the way in between, how can the "why?" below be connected? So planting this one line slackens the whole flow of text before and after, and on the contrary buries the sutra's purport. And to say that by principle it should be there, one cannot understand what principle is meant; truly ignorant and reckless. One should know that what the Buddha spoke cannot be lightly added to or subtracted from by oneself; how great the audacity. Even if the transmission contains errors, one must have real evidence, and the evidence must further be such that the meaning is truly perfect and precise before one may correct it on that basis. How could one knowingly add what the ancient editions do not have? All who wish to print sutras for merit must know this principle. If such a person does this, not only is there no merit; his offense is very great, because he relies on his own private guesswork, presumes to alter what the Buddha said, and thereby harms the Dharma and harms people. This matter may serve as a blazing warning for a thousand ages, and so I do not shrink from speaking of it incisively.

The Sanskrit word kshanti means peaceful endurance, and is also called patience. "Peaceful endurance" is the general name and "patience" the particular name. "Patience" is accepting in accord, meaning to receive single-mindedly and rightly; "peaceful" is abiding peacefully, meaning that the mind is unmoved; "insult" is injury and insult, that is, the sense of maltreatment. Let us first speak the meaning of the general name, and the particular meaning will appear of itself.

Only when a person can endure does his mind abide peacefully and unmoved. If it is moved, it is not endurance. So the single word "endurance" already contains the sense of abiding peacefully and unmoved. One who studies the Way should, in every place and at every moment, have a mind that is peaceful and unmoved. Hence whatever affair he undertakes, whatever circumstance he meets, whatever dharma he practices, he should receive it single-mindedly and rightly. Spoken of the supramundane Dharma: whatever dharma one practices, if one can rightly receive and peacefully abide in it, that is named endurance. For example, practicing the contemplation that all dharmas are from the first non-arising and attaining the non-arising of deluded thoughts: the mind has rightly received this dharma and abides peacefully and unmoved in it, and so it is named the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. It is also called realizing non-arising, or awakening to non-arising. The word "realize" describes the accepting in accord; the word "awaken" describes the mind's being at peace with the principle. Spoken of the mundane Dharma it is likewise so. As it is said: wealth and honor cannot corrupt him, power and force cannot bend him, poverty and lowliness cannot move him. This is what the ancients called firm endurance. That power and force cannot bend him does not mean stubborn resistance; it means the body may be killed but the will cannot be taken from him. That the will cannot be taken is the mind's abiding peacefully and unmoved; this is precisely what is called patience. This, together with not being corrupted by wealth and honor and not being moved by poverty and lowliness, all shows the mind at peace in the right and unmoved by anything; hence it is called firm endurance. From this one may know that peaceful endurance is the name that covers all: whatever affair one undertakes, whatever circumstance one meets, whatever dharma one practices, one should rightly receive and peacefully abide. Patience, then, is one matter within peaceful endurance. Hence it is said that peaceful endurance is general and patience is particular. One should know that whenever patience is brought up, the intent is to use the particular to cover the whole, to use the particular to make clear the general. Why? The hardest thing in the world to endure is being insulted without cause. If even this must be endured, one may know the rest. In the sutras and treatises, sometimes the general name is used and sometimes the particular, quite without uniformity. Roughly, the translations of Xuanzang and Yijing both say peaceful endurance, while other translators mostly use patience. People often suspect they are two different dharmas, or debate their relative merit, but in truth though general and particular seem different, their use to make clear the meaning of rightly receiving and peacefully abiding is not different. There is no need to discriminate merit in such places. Taking this occasion to explain the two names in detail makes them easier to hold together.

The sutra text does not say "patience" but says "the paramita of patience," which shows that in patience one can practice prajna. Why? Because without prajna it is not called a paramita. And to be able to practice prajna is to be able to illumine the nature and be free from marks; hence it says that what the Tathagata says is not the paramita of patience. Why one should be free from marks, the text below precisely explains.
(Yin) 2. Citing proof. In two parts: (Mao) 1. Citing an affair of the present kalpa; 2. Citing affairs of many lives.
(Mao) 1. Citing an affair of the present kalpa.

["Why? Subhuti, as when I was in the past cut limb from limb by King Kali. At that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why? When in former times my body was dismembered joint by joint, had I had the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, I should have given rise to hatred."]

"Why?" is his own hypothetical question as to why patience should be free from marks. The citation of the factual case is meant to prove that patience must be free from marks. The affair of King Kali belongs to the present kalpa, which is named the Bhadra kalpa, the Good Kalpa, because a thousand Buddhas appear in it and there are very many sages and worthies; hence the name.

The word "kalpa" has two meanings: (1) an extremely long period of time; (2) a calamity. Here it is the first meaning. What is called "the present kalpa" refers to a great kalpa. Every great kalpa divides into four middle kalpas, named formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness. The world's having formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness is like beings' having birth, old age, sickness, and death. Every middle kalpa again divides into twenty small kalpas. In each small kalpa, at the time when beings' life-spans are at their shortest, most have only ten years. At that time beings are utterly evil and life is utterly bitter; hardly any of the things that sustain life are produced, and whatever is produced is a thing that destroys life. All this is brought about by evil karma. Hence the number of such beings is also extremely small. The sutras say that the population of Jambudvipa at that time was no more than ten thousand in all. In the extremity of suffering they think of good and gradually turn back, and their life-spans gradually increase. But the increase is very slow, because their turning back toward good is not a forward leap but a gradual tending toward the road of good. Roughly, a hundred years pass before one year is added. Increasing gradually in this way, by the time ordinary life-spans reach twenty years, more than a thousand years have already passed. Seeing that doing good brings good reward, more and more people do good. The things that sustain life gradually multiply, the population gradually increases, and every hundred years one year is added. Adding one year every hundred years until ordinary life-spans reach eighty-four thousand years, the increase has reached its utmost and happiness has reached its utmost. At the extremity of joy sorrow is again produced, because the good mind gradually diminishes. Then one year is subtracted every hundred years. Subtracting one year every hundred years until ten years are reached, the decrease has reached its utmost; then they again turn back toward good and increase, and so enter the second small kalpa. And its one increase and one decrease continue cycling in this way. Kalpa after kalpa it is thus: one year added every hundred years, from ten years up to eighty-four thousand years, and again one year subtracted every hundred years, down to ten years. Reckoned thus, the length of every small kalpa is sixteen million seven hundred ninety-eight thousand years. Eighty small kalpas make one great kalpa, so the length of one great kalpa is one billion three hundred forty-two million eight hundred forty thousand years. Yet at a glance, though it is said to be more than a billion years, in fact at the time of the kalpa of formation the world is not yet complete, and at the time of the kalpa of decay the world is already gradually decaying; even if there are beings in the world then, their suffering may be imagined. At the time of the kalpa of emptiness there is not yet this world, so how could there be beings? The sutras say that when the world meets the kalpa of decay, the Buddha by his spiritual power moves the beings of this world to other worlds. Only a single kalpa of dwelling is a complete world, and even from it one half of the kalpa of decrease must be removed. The time when life-spans increase and beings are happy and at ease is no more than the kalpa of increase within the kalpa of dwelling, one hundred sixty-seven million nine hundred eighty thousand years. Even if one has the long life of eighty-four thousand years, in the end one cannot escape the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Think carefully: what is there in this world to cling to? So taking this occasion to explain the state of this world in detail, it is best for the great assembly to awaken quickly.

Our World-Honored One was born in the ninth kalpa of decrease within the kalpa of dwelling, when ordinary life-spans were a hundred years down to seventy or eighty. Counting to the present, nearly three thousand years have passed. So the life-span today is seventy at the most, and forty or fifty is most common; this is what is constantly seen in the newspapers. Reckoned by the sutras' saying that one year is subtracted every hundred years, it is in fact not far from the facts, which is enough to prove that the Buddha's words are not false. Now and then there are those who pass a hundred years, but they are exceedingly few; there must be some special good cause for this, and it is an exception. Hereafter it will decrease still further and life will grow still more bitter. So one who lives at this juncture can only urge the great assembly to take refuge together in the Buddha Dharma. If there can be a great many people who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, the world will at once be at peace. One who plants good causes will surely obtain good fruit. Though this is the kalpa of decrease, it is not impossible to see an exceptional flourishing. The Buddha says that all is made by mind alone, and again that all dharmas are nothing but illusory marks. So whether life-spans are many or few, and whether the world's affairs are in order or in chaos, though there is a fixed number, in truth the fixed is not fixed; it lies in what people do. One should further urge all to arouse the great compassionate mind, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, seek rebirth in the Pure Land, and obtain a final settlement. Then for the world and beyond the world there is a way. To repay the Buddha's kindness is here, to save all suffering is here, to fulfill the bodhi vow is here; I wish to encourage you all together in this.

"Formerly" and "in the past" make clear that this was a matter of former lives. At that time the World-Honored One was manifesting the body of a bodhisattva and practicing the bodhisattva path. "Was cut" means "was subjected to." Kali is Sanskrit; in the sutras it is sometimes written Kalafu, sometimes Kalinga, sometimes Katri, all being this same person. Its translated meaning is "evil king," like what China calls a benighted ruler. Kali was at that time king of the city of Kusinagara in southern India. He was cruel by nature and delighted in doing poisonous and vicious things, and so gained this evil name. At that time the bodhisattva, for the sake of beings, was sitting in meditation in the mountains. One day the king led his consorts on an outing in the countryside, and being weary he rested a while. The women went to gather flowers and so came to the place of meditation. The bodhisattva, wishing to cut off their greed, spoke the Dharma for them. The king suddenly came looking for them with sword in hand and angrily demanded: Why do you use magic to lure my women? The bodhisattva said: I keep the pure precepts and have long been without a defiled mind. The king said: Have you attained the fruit of arhatship? He said: No. The king said: Have you attained the fruit of non-return? He said: No. The king said: You are young; since you have attained no fruit, you possess greed, so why look upon my women? He answered: Though I have not cut off the fetter of greed, my mind is truly without greed. The king said: Even sages who live on air and eat fruit still feel greed at the sight of form, how much more you in the prime of youth. He answered: To see form without greed does not come from living on air and eating fruit; it comes from fixing the mind on impermanence and impurity. The king said: To slight and slander another, how can one be called a precept-keeper? He answered: Where there is envy there is slander; where there is no envy there is no slander. The king said: What is called a precept? He said: Endurance is called the precept. (From this one may know that unless the mind peacefully abides in the precepts, it is not called precept-keeping.) The king then cut off his hands, feet, ears, and nose with his sword and said: Do you still endure? He answered: Even if the great king were to divide my remaining substance into atoms, I could still endure and would not give rise to a thought of hatred. The ministers all remonstrated, but the king's anger did not cease. Then the four heavenly kings rained down diamond sand. The king, seeing it, was terrified and knelt long in repentance. The bodhisattva made a vow: If I truly have no thought of hatred, let this body of mine be restored as before. Having made this vow, his body was at once restored. He further made a vow, saying: In a future life I will first ferry the great king. Therefore when I now became a Buddha I first ferried Kaundinya, for this king was Kaundinya in a former life. This affair is found in the Mahaparinirvana Sutra and the Vibhasa, with differences in detail; I have gathered them and cited them together. What this sutra calls being cut limb from limb refers precisely to the sword cutting off ears, nose, hands, and feet.

It was said above that if one grasps at the mark of dharma, one grasps at self, person, being, and life. So the present words "no mark of self" and the rest make clear that he does not grasp at the mark of the dharma of patience. That it does not say "no mark of patience" but says "no mark of self" and the rest is because only without the marks of self and others can one not grasp at the mark of patience; this makes clear that discriminating self from others is the root of the disease of grasping at marks. Without the discrimination of self and others, the mind is peaceful and unmoved, and so one can let oneself be cut limb from limb and endure this extraordinary insult. Hence it says: At that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. "At that time" means "at that moment," that is, when he was formerly cut limb from limb. One should know that to endure this extraordinary insult is what others see as so; the bodhisattva at that time was as though nothing had happened, and there was no such thing as insult or no insult, endurance or no endurance. This is what is called patience that is not patience. To see that patience is not patience is precisely the right wisdom of prajna. Hence inwardly he did not see one who endures, and so had no mark of self; outwardly he did not see what is endured, and so had no mark of person. The bodhisattva sat in meditation, his original aim being to realize the Way in order to ferry beings. Now he let others cut him limb from limb, forgetting even this matter and putting life and death outside his concern; hence it says no mark of a being and no mark of a life. This is because the bodhisattva possessed the right wisdom of prajna, and so penetrated the one true dharma-realm. In the one true dharma-realm how could there be any such marks of opposition as self and other, being and Buddha, birth and death? Hence the four marks are all absent. With the four marks all absent, the ten thousand thoughts are all still. What is called insult, and what is called endurance? Only after this could he endure this extraordinary insult. Knowing this, one knows that no gate of practice can be accomplished without reliance on prajna. Knowing this, one knows that no cultivator, without reliance on prajna, can be without obstruction, can attain freedom, can reach the other shore. Hence it says that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment all come forth from this sutra; hence it says that wherever it is taught as occasion arises, all gods and humans should make offering, and that wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha, or a venerable disciple. Hence whoever hears and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, and teaches it to others, even a four-line verse, all accomplish what is rare and obtain immeasurable merit and virtue. Even if people in the world cannot all accomplish it thus, if only the discrimination of self and other is somewhat lightened, then contention will surely lessen, and the world will at once be at peace, with all dwelling in security and joying in their work. Therefore prajna is the true spirit of Buddhism and the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma. All beings should revere and honor it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, and never for a moment be apart from it.

The second "why?" asks why one should be free from the four marks. "Joint by joint" means "segment by segment." "To dismember" is to break apart; "to cut" is to dissect; both mean to analyze and divide. To analyze segment by segment refers to the hands, feet, ears, and nose being cut off one by one. "I should have given rise to hatred" shows by contrast that he could not have endured. Consider that at that time, suffering this extraordinary insult without cause, had he not been entirely without the discrimination of self and others and with all ten thousand thoughts empty, how could he possibly not have given rise to hatred?

Someone may say: that at that time he vowed to be restored and was at once restored as before means he must have had spiritual powers, and so could endure the pain; how could an ordinary being do it? This view is utterly mistaken; it is a perverse view and must be refuted. One should know that even one who has attained spiritual powers and can bear pain, if a thought of hatred arises, will surely be unable to endure it. Why? Because spiritual powers have nothing to do with hatred. Even those who are full of greed, anger, and delusion, like evil demons, can obtain powers. This is why the Buddha Dharma does not value spiritual powers. Though the Buddhas and bodhisattvas sometimes manifest spiritual powers, it is to express the Dharma, or to convert stubborn and darkened beings when there is no other way, and only now and then. In practice one does not emphasize them.

Moreover, this sutra cites this story to make clear that the unsurpassed bodhi takes great kindness and great compassion as its root, and so one must be free from the marks of discriminating self and others, causing the mind to give rise to not a single thought and to abide peacefully and unmoved. Only then can one obtain equality between gratitude and enmity and accomplish the samadhi of great compassion. When this samadhi is accomplished, one can then, even meeting the greatest adverse circumstances and evil conditions, give rise to no hatred. With hatred utterly absent, one can then ferry all beings and fulfill the bodhi vow. Why? Because beings are stubborn and hard to ferry. Hence the bodhisattva's practice of patience has this as its aim. How could one who merely has spiritual powers even dream of it? Otherwise, consider what is said below: to give body and life as many as the sands of the Ganges three times a day. One can know that such a person has the greatest spiritual powers. Such a person fears no hardship and is exceedingly hard to match; yet he is not equal to one who hears this sutra and whose faith does not oppose it. Why? It makes clear precisely that if one does not believe, understand, receive, and uphold the prajna Dharma-gate, the discriminating mind surely cannot be thoroughly relinquished. If the discriminating mind is not pure, one has not reached the one true dharma-realm or realized the empty and still nature-substance; then one can by no means accomplish the unconditioned great kindness and the great compassion of one substance. Even if one can give up immeasurable, boundless bodies and lives, it is still with outflows, and one may still retreat upon meeting conditions. Why? Because not having reached the one true and empty and still, one's ignorance is not yet cut off, and so one's root of faith is not yet accomplished. Therefore one who has spiritual powers, even if he can be patient, is fundamentally utterly different from a bodhisattva's ability to be patient; how could they be mentioned together? Hence below he further cites affairs of many lives to prove that patience is no easy matter; unless one has long studied prajna and attained the great emptiness-samadhi, one may suddenly meet the greatest adverse circumstance and evil condition, and with the least stirring of hatred lose all one's former work. That is why one who upholds and teaches this sutra has merit surpassing that of one who gives up bodies and lives as many as the sands of the Ganges; the reason lies here. In sum, it makes clear that without practicing the prajna Dharma-gate one cannot be free from all marks or accord with the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and in the end cannot accomplish the bodhisattva of great kindness and great compassion. To know thus is right knowledge; to see thus is right view.

As for vowing to be restored and being at once restored as before, there are three meanings, each deeper than the last. (1) Because of the Buddha's empowering. This is why a vow, once made, is fulfilled. (2) Because of great compassion. This is why he received the Buddha's empowering. Consider that after being cut limb from limb he vowed that in a future life, when he became a Buddha, he would first ferry the great king. One can see that the reason he had not a trace of hatred was that he had already attained the samadhi of great compassion. How is that samadhi attained? By being without a discriminating mind. (3) Because of purity of mind. This is why he was without a discriminating mind and attained the compassion-samadhi.

For in studying prajna one contemplates the one true dharma-realm, neither mark nor non-mark, and one's work becomes deep and mellow and the one mind is pure. Because the mind is pure, the dharma-realm is pure. At this time the power of the compassionate vow is great and boundless, and whatever vow is made is at once accomplished. To call it the empowering of all Buddhas is all right; to call it what is manifested by mind alone is also all right. Why? Because one has already realized that mind, Buddha, and beings are three without difference. If one speaks of spiritual powers, this is precisely the great spiritual power of the Buddhist gate, what is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows. How could that which has outflows be mentioned in the same breath?

The former passage (that is, what follows the first "why?") makes clear that being free from marks is what enables one to accomplish the dharma one practices; that is, being free from the mark of dharma is precisely what accomplishes the mark of dharma. The latter passage (that is, what follows the second "why?") makes clear that not being free from marks is precisely what destroys the dharma one practices; that is, not being free from the mark of dharma makes it become the mark of non-dharma instead. The former passage makes it clear from the front; the latter reveals it from the reverse. Taking the front and the reverse together, is it not that being free from the mark of dharma is precisely being free from the mark of non-dharma? In simple terms, being free from marks is what keeps one from falling into emptiness, and not being free from marks is what makes one fall into emptiness. To unfold this meaning is precisely to deal a blow on the head to the fearful. For the fearful suspect nothing but that being free from marks must fall into emptiness; now they know it is precisely the opposite. Such a refutation is incomparably sharp. And with this, the meaning of prajna's freedom from marks is unfolded to the point where nothing remains unrevealed. Yet had the World-Honored One not thus skillfully brought it out, who could have clearly understood? If this meaning is not clearly understood, then one's grasp of freedom from marks is never thorough, and in the end one cannot avoid moments of doubt. So one who, hearing this sutra, can be neither startled nor terrified nor afraid must have deeply understood this meaning; he is truly most rare.

From this one sees that though the text above says only "is not the paramita of patience," it already contains the sense of "is named the paramita of patience." So one can see that when the Buddha speaks the Dharma, he says it on this side while the meaning penetrates the other side, and every side is complete. One may further awaken to the fact that wherever "is not" and "is named" are raised together, though the words stand side by side, the meaning truly leans to the side of "is not." To make this meaning clear in other words: was it not said above that "is not" is spoken by way of the nature, and "is named" by way of marks? Yet the nature is the root and marks are the branches. Only with the root are there branches; because of emptiness, existence appears. So one knows that one should lean to the side of "is not." Hence being free from the mark of dharma is precisely being free from the mark of non-dharma. This is the meaning of what was said above, that the Buddha Dharma takes prajna as master and takes emptiness as master. Why? Because the nature-substance is from the first empty and still. This is why the Buddhas and bodhisattvas take the great emptiness-samadhi as ultimate, and why with no wisdom and no attainment they attain the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment; and though they attain it, they still have no wisdom and no attainment. Why? Because with the least attainment, one has still not attained.

That the Buddha says one should have given rise to hatred is not only to unfold the meaning spoken above; there is a further essential meaning that must be made clear. One should know that hatred is the great taboo of a cultivator. The World-Honored One, wishing to warn those who arouse the bodhi mind, teaches that no matter at what time, in what circumstance, or in what practice, one must absolutely not give rise to hatred; and he uses patience here as the occasion to make it clear. That he speaks of it with reference to patience is because patience very easily gives rise to hatred, and once hatred arises the practice of patience is destroyed, and such matters and principles are easy for people to understand. Speaking by way of what is easy to understand, as an example, so that one may comprehend all, this is the Buddha's subtle intent. Do not misunderstand it to mean that only in patience may one not give rise to hatred while in other matters it does not matter.

Why is hatred the great taboo of cultivation? Because hatred is precisely in conflict with bodhi. Bodhi is enlightenment, equality, compassion. Hatred arises because things do not go as one wishes, which is grasping at self; where then is equality? The affairs of the world are all dream and illusion; why take seriously whether things go as one wishes or not? If one does not know this, where is enlightenment? That it contradicts compassion needs no saying. So once the mind of hatred arises, the seed of bodhi is utterly destroyed. A cultivator who forgets and loses bodhi will, if it is light, grow slack and let his practice decay, and if it is heavy, lose his mind of the Way entirely. Even if he does not retreat, to practice with a mind of hatred can never accomplish the right fruit. The Buddha says: to forget and lose the bodhi mind while cultivating all good is to be held by demons. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva says: among the faults of a bodhisattva none is greater than hatred; though the merit formerly accumulated be as many as a forest, if the fire of hatred arises it is all burned away at once. Both are found in the Avatamsaka Sutra. Should one not fear? Should one not fear? One should know that of the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, delusion is the root of the poison, and delusion is ignorance. From ignorance arise greed and anger. And of the two poisons of greed and anger, the poison of anger does the greater harm. Why? Because its nature is violent. If it does not break out, well and good; but when it breaks out, one will not even pause to consider that one is utterly reversing all one's former conduct. So the cultivator should strictly guard against it. The Buddha spoke this sutra to open the right wisdom of beings and cure delusion; he speaks of giving at the sutra's opening to cure greed; and hatred was not yet spoken of, so he specially supplies it here. Above he said that in practicing giving one should be without dwelling in dharmas; here he says that giving rise to hatred comes from having the four marks. Both make clear that unless one opens the right wisdom of prajna to cure the delusion of grasping at marks, greed and anger cannot be removed. "Should have given rise to" means that it must inevitably follow. Once one grasps at marks, one is bound to give rise to hatred; once hatred arises, all one's practice is bound to be destroyed. Therefore a cultivator who does not study prajna cannot but have a mind like space in every place and at every moment. This is the original intent of the Buddha's speaking of this section. How could it be so only for patience?

One should know that all affairs in the world are nothing but opposition. (Such as cause and effect, self and other, male and female, yin and yang, birth and death, order and chaos, and even defilement and purity, prosperity and decline, suffering and joy, and so on; there is not one affair outside opposition.) Because of opposition, discrimination and calculation very easily arise. Since the common eye takes all oppositions as real things, discrimination and calculation become unbreakable. This is why there is greed and hatred. If one can, within opposition, see the principle of waxing and waning, increase and decrease, and adjust and adapt it to govern all the affairs of the world, one cannot but concede that such a one is a sage of the world. Yet though he can make use of opposition, in the end he cannot leap outside the circle of opposition. The Buddha Dharma is not so. Since all is nothing but opposition, one sees through it here: all of it is nothing but arising through the mutual contrast of this and that. Since all are matters of mutual contrast, all are illusory and unreal, and existence is precisely non-existence. Yet it is not that there is no illusory manifestation, which is non-existent yet existing. So one transcends its surface and is not bound by it, and yet one still accords with what is within it and does not abolish its affairs. To transcend its surface is non-grasping; without this one cannot realize the absolute nature-substance: this is great wisdom. To accord with what is within it is non-destruction; without this one cannot save the beings of the round of rebirth: this is great compassion. All Mahayana sutras speak this principle, and prajna speaks it in especial detail; the Diamond Prajna speaks it in especial subtlety.

One who studies Buddhism and can see as far as this is said to have opened the eye of the Way. If the eye of the Way is opened, one should at once nourish one's mind of the Way. How to nourish it? One should make the mind like space, transcending the dust. To be like space is to not dwell in marks. The sutra says that giving without dwelling in marks has merit like space; its meaning is precisely to make one free from marks so that the mind becomes like space. One must have the emptiness of beings and the emptiness of dharmas, and then the mind is empty. The emptiness of beings does not mean that there is no self, person, or being, but that one does not grasp at their marks. The emptiness of dharmas does not mean that there are no dharmas; the dharmas one should practice one still practices one by one in accord with the Dharma, but one acts as though nothing were happening. Practicing giving, one forgets that it is giving; practicing patience, one forgets that it is patience; even practicing the six paramitas, one forgets that they are the six paramitas. "As though nothing were happening" and "forget" mean not grasping at the marks of the one who acts and the act. This is the double emptiness of self and dharma, and the emptiness of emptiness as well.

For a beginner this is certainly not easy to reach, but one must not shrink from the difficulty; one must constantly comprehend this meaning and make one's mind empty and hollow: this is the essential point. To transcend the dust is not to mingle with all the opposing affairs and principles of the dusty world, and constantly to keep in the mind an intent to break free, never letting it lapse: this is the essential point. One should know that only by not mingling can the mind gradually become empty. And at this point one should raise the one phrase, the great name of ten thousand virtues, and recite it single-mindedly, without discriminating who is reciting and who is the Buddha, only letting the recitation be the Buddha and there be no recitation outside the Buddha. This mind has already been made like space, so this thought that is the Buddha also fills space, and above it is in breath-to-breath communion with the Tathagatas of the ten directions and below with the beings of the dharma-realm. Thus one may call it having thoughts or call it having no thoughts; may call it the Buddha being the thought and the thought being the Buddha; may call it the Buddha and the beings being in this mind; may call it this mind being without difference and without mark from the Buddha and the beings. One should further read and recite the Diamond Prajna Paramita much, to perfume and nourish it, so that the eye of the Way opens day by day and the mind of the Way grows firm day by day. This is the method of cultivating prajna and the Pure Land together. This method accords with the one true dharma-realm, accords with the true mark, accords with non-grasping at emptiness and existence and the perfect fusion of nature and mark, accords with the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and also accords with the meaning that when the mind is pure the land is pure. Try it, and you should find it beneficial. For this is to follow the opposing dharma of cause and effect and yet cultivate the absolute, surpassingly wonderful cause, and so realize the absolute, surpassingly wonderful fruit.

In the sutra above there are many places that speak of being without the four marks of self and person, but all are spoken from the front side, that is, by way of the benefit gained. Where harm is spoken of from the reverse side, there is only what is said at the sutra's opening: if one has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then one is not a bodhisattva. Yet that states what must be so. Now, saying that one should have given rise to hatred states why it must be so. Why? Because if hatred arises, it is not the bodhi mind, that is, not enlightenment, and one is still a deluded ordinary being wandering on the wrong road; hence it says he is not a bodhisattva. From this one may know that one who wishes to leave the wrong road and be born in the Pure Land, how can he fail to give attention to the double emptiness of self and dharma? For whether one grasps at the mark of self or at the mark of dharma, with the least discrimination and calculation one is dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind. If the mind is defiled by dust, how can it be pure? If the mind is not yet pure, the Pure Land is not born. Be careful not to say that the Pure Land Dharma-gate need not speak loftily of prajna.

The Buddha's words are indeed perfectly wondrous and should be viewed from every side. And the dharmas the Buddha spoke are likewise without exception perfectly wondrous and should also be viewed from every side. For of the dharmas the Buddha spoke, there is not one that does not contain many dharmas, and so many dharmas can again return and converge in one dharma. This is why the Avatamsaka makes clear the meaning that one is all and all is one. Hence this sutra says there is no fixed dharma, and so it must not be grasped. As was said above, giving contains all six paramitas; one should know that patience too contains all six paramitas. As it is said, endurance is called the precept, so the paramita of patience is the paramita of precepts. That he let himself be cut limb from limb and thereby formed the condition for ferrying the king in a future life is to make patience into giving. That hatred does not arise and he accepts in accord is meditative concentration. Why? Accepting in accord and unmoved, is that not concentration? And because of concentration he does not give rise to hatred. And the text below says five hundred lives of patience, which is vigor. That being without the marks of self and others is prajna needs no saying. So citing the paramita of patience gathers in all the remaining paramitas. Extending this to all the paramitas, each is so. Hence though this sutra does not plainly speak of vigor and meditative concentration, they are in fact already contained within giving and patience.

One should know that the three paramitas of precepts, vigor, and concentration cannot easily be accomplished apart from the two paramitas of renunciation and patience. Why? Keeping the precepts depends on accepting the precepts in accord and renouncing defiling conditions. The accomplishment of concentration too depends on renouncing torpor and distraction and rightly receiving without moving. And if one cannot renounce and cannot endure, what vigor could there be to speak of? So the two paramitas of giving and patience are truly the mainstay of all gates of practice. This is why this sutra cites only giving and patience.

Again, giving is what is called renunciation. If one grasps at marks, one will certainly be unwilling to renounce, just as one who grasps at marks certainly cannot endure. That one cannot but study prajna is most clear. Hence this sutra takes only these two paramitas to make clear freedom from marks. Since these two paramitas are the mainstay of the gates of practice, if these two can be free from marks, the remaining gates of practice will naturally be free of grasping.

That giving is spoken first and patience afterward also holds a deep meaning. For renunciation has the power to sweep away grasping and to break the self, and is most closely bound up with prajna. It was said above that one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit can give rise to faith and take this as real; this too is to make one who studies prajna first learn to renounce. For keeping the precepts is to renounce all defiling conditions and former evil habits, and cultivating merit means one should give and renounce. First making one learn this practice of renunciation in order to sweep away grasping and break the self, one can then increase the seeds of prajna. This is why one can give rise to faith in these phrases and take them as real. This is why giving should be spoken first. And keeping the precepts is the study of precepts; being able to give rise to faith and take this as real is the study of wisdom. Judging by the surface of the text, the two studies of precepts and wisdom are already present, but concentration is not yet spoken of. The work of concentration is accomplished only through patience, so when directly making clear the rare accomplishment, he gives a hint by way of the paramita of patience, so that one may know that to become a bodhisattva one must be completely equipped with the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Yet only by being free from marks can one accomplish patience; this is why patience is spoken last. From this one may know that what are called the six paramitas, spoken of by way of affairs and marks, are six in number, but in meaning they complete one another and are closely related, and in practice must be one continuous thread. How is this shown? Precepts are the foundation of practice because their function is to renounce the defilement of former habits; and renunciation is the meaning of giving. The meaning of keeping the precepts is that the mind can accept the precepts in accord and abide peacefully in them; hence it is said that endurance is called the precept. And accepting in accord and abiding peacefully is the mind's being concentrated and unmoved. Only when one accepts in accord with the dharma contemplated with a single mind does wisdom arise; hence it is said that concentration gives rise to wisdom. Yet one must also possess the wisdom that sweeps away grasping and breaks the self before one can accomplish the concentration that abides peacefully and unmoved. For prajna is the mother of the paramitas, and all gates of practice are born of contemplative wisdom; so concentration too cannot be outside this principle. Concentration and wisdom are mutually arising. If with respect to prajna, giving, keeping the precepts, patience, and meditative concentration one is unwearied and does not retreat in each, that is vigor. Why can one be unwearied and not retreat? Because one receives each dharma single-mindedly and rightly and abides peacefully and unmoved in it, and because one renounces each dharma as soon as it is attained and never grasps at marks or is self-satisfied. Thus one sees that every dharma gives rise to and contains every other. If one is lacking, all six fail. The practitioner must not fail to understand this principle.

Among all gates of practice, the two paramitas of renunciation and patience are certainly the mainstay, and renunciation is the mainstay within the mainstay. How do we know this is so? Consider that this sutra speaks of patience in only one or two places (here, and the later phrase "accomplished in patience"), while it speaks of giving most often. What is the meaning? Because renunciation can sweep away grasping and break the self, and so can best dissolve karma and remove obstacles and best reveal the right wisdom of prajna. From this one may know that in the ocean of the Buddha Dharma, renunciation is the vanguard (as at the very beginning one must keep the precepts and cultivate merit in order to learn renunciation) and is also the rearguard (as at the end one does not dwell even in the unsurpassed bodhi). And the practice of patience too cannot be accomplished without renunciation. To let oneself be cut limb from limb, is that not renunciation? Not only this: not grasping at dharmas or non-dharmas is to renounce everything. When renunciation is complete, one is thus and unmoved, and is accomplished in patience. One should know it thus.
(Mao) 2. Citing affairs of many lives.
["Subhuti, I also recall that in the past, through five hundred lives, I was a patient sage. In all those lives I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life."]

"In the past" refers generally to the time before King Kali. What the sutras call a sage refers generally to all cultivators and does not specifically mean non-Buddhists; hence the Buddha is also translated as the Golden Sage. It was said above that whenever patience is brought up, the intent is to use the particular to make clear the general; so wherever there is not an explicit fact of insult, it should be understood in the sense of peaceful endurance. The patience spoken of in this section does not necessarily mean that all five hundred lives were like the affair of King Kali. Moreover, when the World-Honored One practiced the bodhisattva path, the bodies and lives he gave were beyond counting; how could it be only five hundred lives? This is merely a brief mention. As when for the sake of one line or half a verse of Dharma he gave up his life and body; or burned his body as an offering to the Buddha; or cut his flesh to light a lamp; and also cut his thigh to save a dove, or gave his body to feed a tiger, and so on. In every case it was above for the Buddha Dharma and below for beings. To say now that for five hundred lives he was a patient sage is meant to make clear that through many lives and many births he gave up life, all the while acting as though nothing were happening, his mind peacefully enduring and unmoved. "All those" means "so many," referring to the five hundred lives. That through so many lives he could peacefully endure was because through so many lives he practiced the prajna Dharma-gate of freedom from marks. Hence it says, in all those lives, no mark of self and so on.

Citing affairs of many lives is meant to prove that his ability to endure peacefully in the affair of meeting King Kali above was due to long cultivation of prajna, so that those who arouse the bodhi mind and practice the bodhisattva path may have something to follow. In sum, prajna at the gate of contemplation and renunciation and patience at the gate of practice are the essential gate of studying the Way. Why? Beings are beings because they have the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion. Prajna cures delusion, renunciation cures greed, patience cures anger. But the root of the disease of the three poisons is very deep: unless one cultivates renunciation much, how can greed be broken? Unless one cultivates patience long, how can anger be removed? Yet unless one finely cultivates prajna and is equipped with the wisdom of the three emptinesses to remove the folly of grasping at marks and discriminating, then renunciation and patience too can never be accomplished, and the three paramitas of precepts, vigor, and concentration will have the name but not the reality. Therefore the Diamond Prajna cites renunciation and patience alone to make clear freedom from marks, so that one may know that grasping at marks is the three poisons and that one should therefore be free from marks through renunciation and patience and so uproot them. If the three poisons are uprooted, the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom are complete, and the three bodies of dharma, reward, and response can be manifested as well. Then the three paramitas of prajna, giving, and patience are the very brain of the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices, and the practitioner should know where to put his first effort.

In the section above on the first paramita, it is said that being free from the mark of dharma is also being free from the mark of non-dharma; this unfolds the meaning that though empty it is truly not empty. In the section on patience, it is said that being free from the mark of dharma is precisely being free from the mark of non-dharma; this unfolds the meaning of accomplishing non-emptiness through emptiness, which is also the meaning of not empty yet empty. From this one may awaken to the fact that wherever the sutra says "not," it is precisely to accomplish what "is"; and wherever it says "is," it is precisely to give shape to what is "not." Hence it says there is no fixed dharma, and therefore one should not dwell in any dharma. One should know that all mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas are without exception thus empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty. So while each is plainly manifest as existing, each is in truth at that very moment empty; and while each is at that very moment empty, each is in truth plainly manifest as existing. This is what is called the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. Hence no single dharma may be grasped as truly non-existent, nor grasped as truly existent. Hence it says that whatever has marks is false and delusory. Why? Because since none is other than false and delusory, it is not truly existent; and since it is not that there is no false and delusory, it is not truly non-existent. So dharmas and non-dharmas alike cannot be spoken and cannot be grasped. Where there is grasping, it is due to nothing else than the marks of opposition and discrimination of self and others in the mind. Hence it says that if the mind grasps at marks, it is grasping at self, person, being, and life. And if the mind discriminates, it is ignorance and is contrary to the equal one true dharma-realm. Hence one who arouses the bodhi mind should not dwell. So the two sections above, unfolding the meaning that what is empty is not empty and what is not empty is empty, are nothing other than a gathered summary of all the meanings spoken before; they have already unfolded the true exposition of non-dwelling to the full. Hence below, taking advantage of this, he makes a comprehensive conclusion and states it plainly: all the words spoken before, all the Dharma-gates, are nothing but true, not deceptive and not different. Why? Because the true suchness, the true mark, is from the first empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty. So all the dharmas it manifests are likewise so. And the dharmas the Tathagata speaks are spoken in reliance on this principle; hence they are called true, hence they are called not deceptive and not different. So the cultivator, with respect to all dharmas, should comprehend and contemplate them thus and be utterly without any dwelling; only then can he not go against the nature, and attain purity of mind and the production of the true mark. If one cannot comprehend and contemplate them thus, ignorance is not broken; hence the words, "like a person entering darkness." If one can comprehend and contemplate them thus, ignorance will surely be broken; hence the words, "the light of the sun shines everywhere." This is to show that all beings, with respect to this Diamond Prajna, cannot but believe, understand, receive, and uphold it.
